FOREWORD

           Underfoot. Underglaze. Understood.



I met Emily in the middle, the beginning, and the future. Emily was
working in the ceramic studio under the defunct football stadium bleachers
in the middle of the country. It was nearly the end of her academic ceramic
education, the beginning of the maker movement and her individual pursuit,
and after our conversation I knew she would attain the future she desired.
We talked about approach, intent, and the possibilities this material presents
for the maker.
  The current reality and empire Emily created was all told to me in
crystal-clear conviction underfoot Wildcat track practice nearly fifteen
years ago. Emily is the perfect guide through the ceramic surface. Her
enthusiasm has driven her curiosity to create and make available the objects
she wants to see and share.
   Plotted and paced out, Emily knew all the steps necessary to create her
current world. It’s important to see it all and then work backward, just like
the ceramic surface. You must know what you’re after but be ready and
willing to abandon the plan in order to better understand possibilities and
opportunities you never knew existed. Allow pauses for growth. Test your
ideas. Forget your ideas. Form new ideas. Remember timing and patience
are necessary in building a ceramic surface and empire. Practice. Repeat.
Continue.
  The ceramic surface can be complex or simple. Don’t worry, there are
rules to help you succeed. Some rules you can break, and some aren’t
flexible at all: Shino first or you’ll be cursed. Shino first or fear the worst.
Shino on top or it’s a flop. Wait—maybe there’s only one rule . . . and who’s
deciding what’s a flop or cursed or the worst? Somehow, we’ve perpetuated
preference as testament instead of fuel to experiment.
   This is where I entered ceramics. In a glaze lab that overflowed with five
hundred options for brown, I wanted pink. I knew I’d never leave when I’d
gained enough glaze chemistry to color-match my cups to the Kool-Aid
they’d contain! Sure, I could have tried to match it with ready-made

commercial glazes, but as a college student, the glaze lab was the only
option out of necessity and economy—the class lab fee covered all of my
curiosity chemistry!
    I’ll never forget the day commercial glazes and underglazes entered my
scene. While preparing a workshop for Kathy King and unpacking the
delivery of commercial products, I understood them as a means to an end,
but also just another ingredient. Commercial products and shortcuts are
traditionally frowned upon; we demonize “easy” in the academic ceramics
community and celebrate complete command, so sharing recipes and
techniques is not a given, it’s gatekeeping. It’s silly, really—truth is, it’s all
for the taking!

Emily has helped to break down these lines, trained academically while
simultaneously adhering to maker-motived efficiency and necessary
consistency. Many of the techniques in this book make use of what’s around
and accessible to you, encouraging you to look at all things differently and
in service to your pottery.

I have been working and teaching in this material for half my life. I’ll
always take the beginning class if given the choice. I love seeing how folks
approach such a versatile medium and often offer little to no instruction
until a question arises. The truth is, we intrinsically know what to do. This
book will be there for your questions and offer assurance of what you
already intuit. The possibilities are exponential and have a magic way of
meeting you where you are and saying: But wait—there’s more!

—Amy Santoferraro
Assistant Professor of Ceramics
California State University, Los Angeles

INTRODUCTION

       You Are an Artist, and This Is an Art Book



I like to think of creativity as an inner flame. It’s housed inside of all of us
the moment we’re born. As we grow and start to discover our inner flame,
where it lives and what it likes, that flame requires attention. Sometimes,
the flame feels so far away that we can have trouble finding it, or it feels
more like a flickering flame than a steady, brilliant light. But it’s there.
We’re never separated from our creative flame. It lives within us always,
and as artists, it’s our job to tend to and strengthen our inner flame.

Yeah, that’s right. You are an artist! I want this section to inspire you to
say, “Yeah, I am creative!” Being creative requires a lot of imagination, a
lot of daydreaming, and lots of research and reading, and you need to be
ready to notice anything and everything around you. Big inspirations and
small inspirations are everywhere, just waiting to be noticed by you. You’ve
got to keep your eyes and your heart open, poised to absorb everything that
lights you up inside. There’s no right way to be creative, and there’s also no
wrong way to be creative. We are all creative.

I visualize ceramic objects and ideas all of the time in my mind’s eye.
When I see something interesting, I think, “How can I build that out of
clay? What would be my approach?” I’ve been a daydreamer from my very
early childhood memories. I remember feeling as though I couldn’t shut off
all of the ideas streaming into my mind and my soul and that I wanted to be
able to move faster bringing these ideas to life. I had very busy hands as a
kid and a very active imagination. I remember hiding a little container of
Silly Putty inside my desk in elementary school. Do you remember Silly
Putty? I had a desk that opened up at my lap, and I would secretly make
tiny little sculptures out of my Silly Putty instead of paying attention in
class. Sure, this was a distraction, but it also feels like a very early sign to
what felt very natural to me, producing tiny Silly Putty works and molding
my ideas into little somethings that kind of resembled objects. How funny
to think that now that’s exactly what I’m doing for a living.

Getting absolutely lost in my creative endeavors is my specialty, and this
state of being feels like my most centered way of existing. What meditation
offers for some people, creation offers me what I would assume is the same
feeling of calm and peace. (I’m not very skilled in meditation.)
  I’m not only losing myself in my creativity, I’m also finding myself in
my creativity. Creativity has the ability to show us who we are. In a big
way, I found myself when I discovered clay. First, I found a community
where I felt I truly belonged. Then, as I started to learn about clay, I also
started to discover those deepest truths about myself and who I am. That
would have never revealed itself had I not listened to my instincts and
followed my interests.

My Path to Ceramics

My clay journey began in 2008 when I enrolled in my first ceramics class at
Kansas State University in Manhattan, Kansas. At the start of my
sophomore year, I was an art education major who really just wanted to be
at a “fancy” art school when I met Amanda Small, my first ceramics
instructor. I give full credit to Amanda for getting me curious and excited
about clay. At the impressionable age of nineteen, in my eyes Amanda was
the artist I wanted to be. We had just finished our first handbuilding project
that semester and our professor Yoshi Ikeda walked into the classroom,
mid-critique. He stood silently in the doorway with his arms crossed,
observing us with a sly grin on his face while he listened to our
conversation. We were all feeling his presence after a while, and on his way
out of the room, he casually stopped by my table, pointed to my sculpture,
said, “That’s pretty good,” and walked away from the room. It was such a
tiny, insignificant compliment, if you blinked you could have missed it.
Amanda spun around and smiled at me, whispering, “Yoshi never says that.
You should change your major to ceramics!”
  A few hours later, with Yoshi’s blessing scribbled on a piece of yellow
legal pad paper (“Emily can be a ceramics major now. –Yoshi”), I marched
to the art department office and presented the note to the office
administrators who reluctantly followed the instructions and made the
appropriate changes in the system. I was officially a ceramics major.
  Once I made my way to the advanced ceramics classes toward my junior
year and I had my own dedicated studio area, I started spending all of my
time at the studio. Yoshi kept a small workspace inside of the advanced
student studios, and throughout the class, he would typically work on his
own work with us. On the weekends, it would often just be me and Yoshi
working together. I remember many Saturday mornings when he would
marvel at the fact that I was there so early, working away. I really just
couldn’t stay out of the ceramics studio, and it was a bonus that he was
there with me.
   That moment Yoshi scribbled his approval of my decision to pursue a
ceramics major on the yellow legal pad would not be the last time Yoshi

would permanently alter the course of my life and my art career. A few
years later, shortly after I graduated from college, Yoshi gave me his kiln
and his wheel and a bunch of other useful studio tools and equipment. He
told me that I had worked hard and he had noticed. He said, “I can teach
someone how to be good at ceramics, but I can’t teach someone how to
have a strong work ethic.” No part of my ceramics career would have
happened without this gift from my teacher. Beyond the equipment, he
showed me he believed in me, and that’s been a driving force for my
creative work ever since.
    I keep a dedicated shrine to Yoshi in my studio. He passed away in 2014,
so I haven’t been able to show him just how significant his gifts were to me,
but my hope is that his legacy will live on within me and the work I do and
that somehow I’ll be able to share some of the powerful gifts of clay know-
how with others—just as my teachers did for me.

My career has taken many different paths, and my art practice is ever-
evolving. I’ve been balancing my two roles as an artist and an entrepreneur
for more than twelve years, with both jobs requiring different things from
me. At one point, I scaled my business up when things started to feel too
busy for just one person, and I scaled it back down once it started to feel
strange having other people make my work for me.

I will feel forever grateful for my art teachers and my experience in the
ceramics department at Kansas State. Led by my professors Yoshi Ikeda
and Dylan Beck, I had a unique experience that I would never trade for
another. While studying with Dylan Beck one semester, I got to apply to be
his student intern. I was able to see firsthand what it means to be a working
artist. Dylan allowed me to go with him and assist with gallery installations
of his work. He taught me how to package and ship ceramic work, how to
make plaster molds and slip cast my work for quicker production of
multiples, and how to think critically about the work I was seeing and the
work I was making, as well as how to apply for art opportunities that would
further my experience in the field. It was the perfect balance to Yoshi’s style
of teaching.
  My art teachers are so special to me. We all deserve to have a teacher
who believes deeply in us, and I was lucky enough to have several art
teachers who impacted me in this way. I’ve always wanted to find a way to
pay it forward and share the knowledge and information that I’ve
discovered and been taught over the years. I hope this book can be my first
chance to share some of what I know and inspire you to fall in love with
ceramics too.

How to Develop Your Artistic Style

For a long time, I didn’t feel like I knew what to make, where to start, or
how to approach fearless creation. To create free of self-doubt requires deep
understanding and a level of confidence that didn’t come naturally to me in
the beginning.





   This is where I channel my deep curiosity.
   Start by noticing more of the world around you. I want you to really dive
deep and discover what inspires you, what catches your attention, and what
lights you up in conversation with others. Recognize what you feel when
this happens and get good at paying attention to the little inspirations that
pop up all the time.
   Find the artists who inspire you the most and read all about them. Find
out everything you can about how they live (or lived), who inspires them,
and the way they started making art. When you find something or someone
that is interesting, dive into that topic or that person and research it until
you find new little nuggets of inspiration and then dive into those!
Inspiration really is endless. You just have to follow the little clues.

Once you’ve gotten the hang of researching and exploring every little
thing that seems like pure magic to you, start getting your hands busy. This
is when I turn to my sketchbook, and I pour myself and my imagination
onto the pages. I start pulling from those people and those things that lit up
the creative spark inside of me, and I start to draw and sketch. Make your
designs your own in some new and exciting way. A spark of inspiration
from one thing can lead somewhere else in your mind, and translating that
to the pages can develop into something completely new.
  Look at and evaluate other ceramic pieces, whether it’s a handmade mug
you bought on vacation years ago, a vintage piece of pottery from the thrift
store, or one of your favorite artist’s works at a gallery or museum. Ask
yourself, “How did they make that? What techniques and materials might
they have used?” Get familiar with the object and critique it as if it were
your own or like you might be viewing it in the artist’s studio. Keep an
inner dialog going on about what you’re seeing and what inspires you.
  Having an idea and being able to execute it takes a lot of practice. Be
prepared to replicate your vision over and over. This is part of the ritual of
creation and making art. Ceramic artists only improve from experience, and
you’ll feel like a beginner for a long time. (I sometimes still feel like a
beginner, and I’ve been working with clay nearly every day for the last
fifteen years!) It feels important to reiterate the point of powering through
and continuing with your creative endeavors despite imperfection. Give
yourself permission to do it badly at first. Perfect doesn’t exist, and striving
for perfection holds you back from fully expressing yourself. So preserve
your creative energy and let your ideas flow until something else grows.
Creators of all kinds stick with it because they feel compelled to keep
going. I feel compelled to make things every single day, and I can’t ignore
this innermost desire.
   Share your creative work with your community. It might feel like no one
is listening, and you might even feel like your work isn’t that important. But
if it’s coming from an honest place inside of you, and if you have something
to communicate through your creative work, that’s important enough. You
can start making judgments about your work on your own so that the work
you produce is unique and true to you, but getting some outside perspective
from friends or other artists is also beneficial for developing a body of work
that you can talk about. Someone close to you might be able to discover

something hidden in your work that you weren’t able to see yet. Talking it
out with other creative people is a helpful way to discover what makes your
style uniquely yours.
    I think regular experimentation is the best way to find your unique
creative voice. The more experiments and tests you amass with a variety of
processes and materials, the more your eye will develop and your style will
start to reveal itself. You’ll find yourself pulled in a certain direction. You
might not know how to articulate why you’re being pulled in that direction,
but over time, it’ll start to make more sense. The picture starts to become
more complete the more you commit yourself to practice.

How to Build and Maintain a Creative Practice

I graduated from Kansas State University in 2010 with my Bachelor of Fine
Arts degree with a concentration in ceramics. After graduation, I turned in
my keys to the ceramics department. I knew when I was leaving school that
finding a way to continue my ceramics practice was a must. It felt crucial to
my existence and to my identity. This was the year before Yoshi gifted
some of his equipment to me, so I needed to find a studio where I could
continue creating.





  Through some friends and word of mouth, I quickly found a ceramic
artist who was hiring a part-time production assistant and I applied. I really
just showed up at her studio one day and told her I was interested in
working for her, and she accepted me on the spot. She was also a former
student of Yoshi Ikeda, and we deeply appreciated that connection to one
another, knowing how special our teacher was. Her home and her studio
were tucked back off the road in a small cluster of trees, and it felt like that
perfectly isolated creative space was secluded in nature, but right on the
edge of town.

I think I worked for her for about twenty hours a week, and I was a
server at a small bar and restaurant when I wasn’t in the studio. Working for
a production potter who had lots of wholesale orders meant we were
producing a lot of work. Proper education on how to make her work was the
first step, and then the thoughtful repetition that comes from making the
same forms over and over was the next step. She graciously allowed me to
work on my own ceramics in her studio during my downtime, and this was
the moment when things started clicking into place for me. I had access to
space, access to a kiln, I had my education and my skills to guide me, and it
was time to push myself creatively and learn all about what it meant to fully
dedicate myself to my studio practice outside of school.
    It was this summer after my graduation that I opened an Etsy shop. I
started listing the work I made in college and, surprisingly, I made some
sales. I kept producing and putting myself out there into the world as
authentically as I could. I created an Instagram account and started
connecting with other artists and ceramicists, and amazingly, it was a
successful social platform for making friends too. I wasn’t shy about
sharing what I was working on, and I think this was hugely beneficial for
me growing as an artist, developing a style, and more importantly,
developing my practice. I show up to my studio every day just as my
teachers did, and I feel incredibly connected to the work and to the ceramics
process.

Find a space to be creative. If that’s a table at your local community
ceramics studio or a potter’s guild in your area, do what it takes to carve out
a space to create in. A rented shelf in a larger communal studio is a great
place to start. My first dedicated studio space was a spare bedroom. Next, I
moved it to a basement, then to a garage, and then to a corner of a large
woodshop. Now, it’s tucked perfectly in the back of my shop and gallery
space that I collaborated with significant people in my life to build and open
and share with a bigger community. It’s an important space that brings me
so many ideas and new discoveries. It’s where my inner creative flame

seems to burn the brightest and the strongest. It took me more than twelve
years to carve out this dream space, so don’t feel pressured to expand on
any sort of timeline other than the one that suits you. Finding a space that
has the tools and equipment to help get you started is all it takes.
    If your creative space is all yours but feels stale, find any way you can to
spruce things up a bit. Maybe that’s a fresh coat of white paint. Maybe it’s
finding the perfect secondhand worktable. Maybe it just needs a quick
tidying up and some organization. Get a small bulletin board to start
pinning up your early sketches and your detailed vision board. If you’ve got
a window, find a little plant or two. Your creative space should make you
feel good, and giving your space a little bit of love before you get started
can help you feel inspired and creatively charged when you walk in the
door.
   Building time into your schedule is also a crucial step in maintaining
your creative practice: time to dream, time to experiment, time to create,
and time to get bored. It’s all part of the creative process that helps you
build your practice in a way that keeps you interested and coming back.
Take time to mess around and take creative risks because these are the
moments that can lead you and your hands somewhere unexpected. When
I’m loading a glaze kiln at my studio, I try to slip in one or two wacky
experiments each time. First of all, it makes unloading the kiln that much
more exciting, not knowing what the results might be when something in
there is a mysterious surprise. And secondly, even your strangest
experiments can lead to creative breakthroughs when it comes to finishing
your work and developing your unique style. This is part of what makes the
discovery process so exhilarating.

Ceramics for Self-Care

Having an artistic hobby or a creative pursuit of any kind is so powerful for
our well-being. It has been shown that creativity improves our mood,
alleviates stress and anxiety, boosts our self-esteem, and broadens our
cognitive abilities. My creative pursuits have led me to important
friendships and incredible opportunities to meet other like-minded, creative
people. Working with clay just feels good, and it’s one of the most-loved
methods I use to take good care of myself.





   Clay requires a lot of physical and mental presence while you’re
working, and so many subtle movements require focus and precision at the
moment. This focus has a way of pulling my mind and my attention away
from the more stressful aspects of life and the worries that are on my mind.
Clay has the ability to keep my hands and my mind active enough for me to
calm myself. Creating something with my hands can make me feel
empowered, and the finished ceramic results are very rewarding too. Clay

gives you a bit of resistance at times, but fighting through that and
continuing the work anyways gives our studio practice power and meaning.
  You don’t have to monetize your creativity. A creative hobby can be
sacred and personal and private and just for you. As a creative entrepreneur
and small business owner, I keep forgetting to make art just for fun—
making art for the sake of art. It’s easy to forget to craft special ceramic
pieces for myself too. Part of what got me into ceramics was the ability to
surround myself with useful and beautiful objects that I created, so don’t
forget to fabricate something just for yourself, without any outside
pressures to turn it into anything. A hands-on artistic hobby is great for self-
care.

Living a Creative Life

I am a collector. I love stuff! That love of stuff led me to name my business
The Object Enthusiast. It has become a big part of my identity. I think a lot
of artists consider themselves collectors as well. I collect things, I collect
art, I collect ideas—my life is filled with these collections. Some are
tangible and some are not, but ultimately, these collectibles have a way of
influencing and encouraging me throughout all areas of my life, not just in
the ceramics studio. I strive to fill my day with anything and everything that
inspires me.

Living a creative life can start the moment we wake up and step out of
bed. For me, that’s when I begin with my coffee routine. My coffee routine
is not just about getting myself caffeinated. That is a big motivator, but not
the only one. My coffee routine helps me feel grounded and more
connected to myself as I begin my day. I start by sourcing quality, ethically
sourced coffee beans. I like using slower, hands-on brewing methods
because it gives me more time to think while I’m preparing the water and
the beans. My kitchen cupboards are filled with handmade ceramic mugs
from my friends and from artists that I’ve never met. When I’m reaching
for a mug, I’m thinking about the person who made it, making part of the
ritual feel more like I’m having coffee with that person.

I have two ceramic mugs that my professor Yoshi made in the 80s that
he gave me one day briefly in passing at the studio. They have tiny glaze
“flaws,” which is why he so willingly gave them to me, I’m sure, but these
aren’t flaws in my eyes. They’re unique characteristics of him as an artist.
They’re marks made by his hands, or his paintbrush, or his glaze recipe, or
his kiln’s atmosphere, completely unique to him and those two mugs. Each
time I reach for the handle, I know my hand is in the exact position and
place that Yoshi’s hand was in when he made the mug and handle, and this
thought sends a charge through my body. These mugs were made
practically forty years ago! Before I was born! But I’m still connected to
him through these two vessels. All these years later, these mugs and my
coffee routine help me feel a deeper connection to my life’s purpose. Yes,
this takes longer than other methods of making coffee in the morning. But it
gives me so much more than just coffee. I’m connecting more to the objects
I live with and the art I’ve collected and to the life I’m living. It means
something to me to spend time like this.
  From the clothes we wear to the food we cook, finding ways to express
ourselves creatively is what it’s all about. When we put care and attention
into some of the more mundane tasks in life, it gives us another opportunity
to notice and appreciate more throughout our day. Leading a creative life
means paying closer attention to the small details that make life worth
living, the things that make our days more interesting and more inspiring
and more joyful. Put a unique and creative spin on a simple task today.
Does it become more interesting? Does it feel a little more special? Don’t
you already feel more inspired? You don’t have to have a reason for putting
a creative spin on something. Do it just for the joy it brings you, or better
yet, the joy it might bring someone else. I love finding small ways to
creatively surprise the people I care about.

Embracing Imperfection

I think my close friends and studio mates like my imperfect work more than
what I deem as “perfection.” This is nice to think about. They appreciate the
pieces I’m creating that don’t quite go as planned, and as a sensitive and
creative soul, that comforts me. It keeps me creating even when I feel
insecure and have a bit of imposter syndrome.
  Do it for the process, not the outcome. I decided a long time ago that I do
not make perfect pots. I am someone who has incredible handwriting one
day and sloppy scribbling the next day. I am a potter who struggles to make
twenty identical cups on the wheel in one sitting. I’ve decided that the small
differences in the pieces I make are what make those pieces interesting, and
it’s part of how I’ve identified my style and my way of mark-making. If I
push too hard for perfection, I just get further from it, and I’ve decided to
embrace the subtle differences that my hand can’t help but make.

Why Ceramic Surface Design Is So Exciting

Surface design is by far my favorite step of the ceramics process. If you’re
the type that loves to experiment and explore and isn’t afraid of repetition,
practice, and just trying something new, you too can embrace surface design
as your favorite part of the process.
  The surface is exciting because it feels like the place where an artist’s
style can start to develop. When I was first starting in ceramics, I had a
small vase that was one of my early favorite pieces I’d made. The shape
was perfect, and I was a proud little potter! Then, I went to glaze it. And
let’s just say, the finished results were not what I was hoping for. This piece
was very brown, and there were lots of spots that didn’t have enough glaze
on them, giving it a streaky finish that I was not in love with. But I kept
holding onto that vase and thinking about what could change. That was the
first time I tried adding gold to the surface of my work. I strategically
covered all those glaze blemishes that I didn’t like with large gold polka
dots, and while the finished vase still wasn’t quite what I wanted, it did lead
me to a new idea. I started exploring how to finish my work with gold, and
I began including this technique into my finishing plans from the earliest
stages of creation. A style emerged from that one experiment, and I had a
new direction to move in.
   What’s also really exciting about surface design is that surface
treatments can be developed at every stage of the ceramics process. Carving
and stamping patterns and texture into leather-hard clay provides a tactile
finish to the surface of your work at the earliest stage. After bisque firing,
the surface can be treated with all types of different glazes for a completely
unique result, and the color and texture combinations are endless. The use
of underglazes and vibrant colors offer another, more painterly approach for
those wanting to include text or imagery on their surface. The possibilities
really are limitless, and that’s what keeps me coming back each time. New
ideas and new ways to approach creating something come to me regularly.

Successful surface decoration consists of both careful planning and a
willingness to embrace the unexpected. There’s an element of surprise when
it comes to experimentation and new tests in the studio. Careful notetaking,
sketching, and planning help when you’re bringing your vision to life and
hoping to re-create it in the future.

   TOOLS AND MATERIALS FOR GETTING STARTED

A ceramic studio setup can look very different from artist to artist, but there are a
number of commonalities among functioning ceramics studios. Your studio might be a
shelf or a dedicated table in a community ceramic studio or it might be modified to fit in
your basement or garage. I’ve had many studios since getting started with clay, and it’s
pretty remarkable to see people making space to create no matter where they are. Clay
enthusiasts have that in common—they can’t help but want to get their hands in clay
and make something, and sometimes that drive to create is so strong that an artist will
transform their dining room table into a temporary work surface if it’s all they have.

THE STUDIO AND SAFETY

If I include my first ceramics studio space when I was in college, I’ve had a
total of nine different studio spaces over the years. Today, my studio sits in
the back of my shop that I opened with my business partner Sasha. It’s
called Duet, and we carry art and objects from other artists, designers, and
brands we admire and believe in. In my studio, I’m working with about 500
square feet (46.5 m2) of workspace, with a little extra for storage and
shipping supplies. I have a ventilated, modest-sized electric kiln, a large
slab roller, a SHIMPO potter’s wheel, a “slop” sink with a clay trap for
catching clay particles, and lots of shelves for holding finished work,
projects in process, and all my tools and materials.
  A clean and organized studio is a safe studio, and it’s important to make
sure your space is well maintained and cared for to protect yourself and the
people who might share it with you. A messy studio makes creative ceramic
work very challenging and potentially dangerous if you’re stepping over a
mess to get to what you’re working on. Now that my space acts as the
backdrop to my shop, it feels even more important to keep it clean and
orderly.

Safety is a big factor when it comes to a workable ceramics studio, so
let’s go over a few safety measures to keep in mind as you’re considering
your studio setup. Communal studios typically have listed guidelines that
all studio members need to follow, but when you’re creating your own
space, it’s important to create some safety guidelines for yourself and stick
to them.
  Avoid excessive dust accumulation by cleaning your studio daily
after every mess and consider doing a weekly mopping or deep cleaning
with a wet vac or HEPA filtered vacuum. I avoid sweeping my studio
whenever possible since it has a tendency to move the dust into the air.
When I’m cleaning my studio, I like to wear a HEPA filter face mask to
avoid any dust inhalation. It’s also helpful to wash your aprons and hand
towels regularly. Any porous fabrics will hold the dust, and it can float back
into the air with quick movements of the fabric.

Most clay bodies contain crystalline silica. When the clay is wet, it’s
mostly harmless. But the moment that clay dries and produces any sort of
dust, that dust becomes airborne and can really harm your lungs if inhaled.
Some moist, prepared clays can have mold present, especially in the bag or
if they’ve been sitting around the studio for a while. If your skin is sensitive
or if you’re prone to allergies, you can try wearing latex or nitrile gloves as
a barrier when working with the clay. Prolonged exposure to clay can dry
your skin, so make sure to keep some good hand soap and lotions on hand
(especially in the wintertime).
   I store my respirator face mask in a large, airtight container so that
it is kept clean and is stored without exposure to more dust when I’m not
using it. You also need to remember to change the filters in your HEPA
filter face mask often. Add a filter-changing schedule to your yearly
calendar so you won’t forget in the future.
  Keep your materials organized and clearly labeled, especially if
you’re working in a studio with hazardous raw materials. Take the time to
educate yourself on what materials are in your clay and glazes. This won’t
always be spelled out for you, so it’s important to do your own research to
keep yourself healthy, safe, and knowledgeable about where your materials
come from.
   I have specific clothes that I wear only in the studio. Most of the
products I’m using are washable, with the exception of some dark clays that
will stain my light-colored clothing. I like to keep my studio clothes and
studio shoes separate from my “nice” clothes when I’m outside of work.
There are always trace amounts of dust and studio debris attached to me as I
move my way through the studio, so I like to make sure I’m not going
straight home and plopping myself on the couch with my dusty clothes. In
the winter, I like to wear a large jumpsuit-style coverall over my clothes as
it’s the perfect thing to keep me fully covered, warm, and prepared for a
creative mess.

TOOLS AND EQUIPMENT

Every artist has their own set of tools and equipment that they rely on to
make their work. Some tools are easily recognizable, while others are
homemade or repurposed objects that serve specific functions in the studio.
Some of the tools in my collection feel very meaningful. I still have my first
beginner’s tool kit from my days as a student as well as some equipment I
inherited from my professor. I enjoy finding new ways to use what I have to
make something new and exciting. As you develop your studio practice,
you’ll start to figure out what tools and equipment you can’t live without.
Here are some suggestions for getting started.





Tools

Tools can be as minimal or as maximal as you’d like. I’ve amassed quite a
large collection of small hand tools over the years, and yet I keep coming
back to the same, simple things time and time again. The two most
important tools for me are my hands, no doubt. What’s most amazing about
clay is that you can do so much with just your hands and some homemade
tools or recycled materials that you turn into tools.

HANDBUILDING TOOLS: If you’re a handbuilder like me, your list of tools
can be pretty simple. Some of my favorite handbuilding tools include a
wire tool, needle tools, varying shapes of carving tools, a set of circle
cookie cutters, stencils, and a ruler.
THROWING TOOLS: A potter’s wheel is essential to start throwing pots,
and a few hand tools help as well. I use silicone and wooden ribs, a
needle tool, a sponge, an angled wooden trimmer, a wire tool, and
various trimming tools. I have small wooden bats that I transfer the
thrown pots to for careful drying before trimming and firing.
FINISHING TOOLS: Glaze application tools can vary from artist to artist. I
keep an assortment of paintbrushes. Lots of different sizes and shapes of
brush heads can make different marks in your glazing. I have squeeze
bottles with different-sized tips. I also like to use a bead rack for glazing
handmade beads and small hanging items and firing stilts for lifting
glazed pieces off the kiln shelf surface.

Equipment

Here’s some of the equipment you’ll see in my studio:

  VENTILATED ELECTRIC KILN: I am most familiar with Skutt kilns, but
   there are many brands to choose from. I use a downdraft vent that pulls
  fumes from the kiln before they can enter the room and vents them
   outside. I keep my kiln shelves and kiln posts carefully stored close by
  the kiln for easy loading and unloading.





  SLAB ROLLER: This was one of the first studio upgrades I made when my
  business began to take off. It was a huge productivity improvement from
  working with a single rolling pin for making a lot of my slab-built work.
  I’m able to roll larger, more consistent slabs for building trays and other
   slab-built objects. It’s also a great work surface for standing work, as I
  love the height of the table.

EXTRUDER: This is also a favorite piece of equipment in my studio. It’s
another one of my cherished gifts from my professor Yoshi. My extruder
was custom built and has different-shaped inserts for creating all kinds of
shaped coils and tubes for handbuilding. I love using it, and it makes
coil-built production work so much easier and faster.

Other Useful Studio Things

Here are some additional supplies that I keep handy in my studio:

  SPONGES OF ALL SHAPES AND SIZES: I use big sponges for cleaning my
  messes, small to medium-sized sponges for cleaning my glazed work or
   refining the surface of my pots, and I love to handcut various tiny sponge
  shapes to use to stamp underglazes or glazes onto the surface for a
   different textured finish.





  A PENCIL AND A RULER: Planning my glaze and surface designs will
  sometimes take some sketching directly on the bisqueware itself. The
  good news is that lead pencil burns out in the kiln, so make as many
  preplanning marks as you need.

WARE BOARDS: I love to use scraps of drywall for my ware boards for
working on and moving my creations. They’re easy to cut into workable
sizes with a box knife, and I finish the edges with painter’s tape or
construction tape. I have a lot of different sizes that I use atop my work
table as a work surface, and then when I wrap my pieces up for careful
drying, I can transport the new creation on the board, getting it safely to
the shelves that hold my works in process.





LARGE SCRAPS OF PLASTIC: I save dry cleaner bags, large sheets of plastic
drop cloths, and recycled bags from my prepared clay to use when I need
to wrap up a work in progress or to loosely cover my clay for slow
drying. Recycled plastic sheets are easy to clean with a damp sponge and
help hold in the moisture of the pieces you’re working on before you’re
ready to dry them out.

BUCKETS OF ALL SIZES: I love one-gallon (3.8 L) buckets. They’re the
perfect size for tabletop work, glaze projects, production work—just
about everything. I keep extra one- and five-gallon (3.8 and 20 L)
buckets on hand for large batches of glaze work, cleaning, and
organizing, as well as recycling my clay scraps.

LIDDED JARS: I use recycled lidded jars for mixing slips and making and
storing small glaze tests. It’s helpful to have lidded containers on hand
for whatever they might become useful for down the road. You never
know!
PLASTER MOLDS: I also use a lot of plaster molds. Different sizes and
shapes of humps and slumps are what I use for much of the tableware
I’m designing. Some of my molds are used for slip-casting my
production designs, while others help me in the handbuilding process.
These molds assist in the building of each form by slowly absorbing the
moisture from the clay so that the pieces can set and hold their form.
They can be removed from the plaster and built upon by hand or refined
and placed on the shelf for careful drying.

MATERIALS

An artist’s preferred materials differ from person to person, and part of the
fun is discovering a new material that inspires creations for you in the
studio. When you’re just getting started, use the basics as a jumping-off
point. Start with one type of clay that you like the appearance of when it is
fully fired. Shop around for two or three commercial glaze colors that
complement the clay you’ve picked out. If you’re in a communal studio,
scout around to see what’s available and begin some tests so that you can
learn what things look like when they’re fired. Once you get more
comfortable in the studio, start experimenting with new options and
finishes. Each time you do, your ideas will expand, and you’ll start thinking
of how to approach your next piece.

Clay

Clay is absolutely essential to any ceramics studio. Keep your clay labeled
and organized when it’s not in use. At times, I’m using eight to ten different
clay bodies in my studio, and keeping them labeled is key so that I don’t
mix them up when I’m working on a commission or a wholesale order. Clay
should never freeze, so you do want to make sure your studio is temperature
controlled, at least in the winter. Do not sand or scrape bone-dry clay on
your drying wares, as this creates a lot of dust particles. It’s a bad habit that
should be avoided. If I’m refining my unfired clay creations, I usually use a
damp sponge so that I’m not creating dust. I’ll discuss a lot more about clay
and how to choose your clay body in chapter 2.

Underglazes

I have somewhere close to forty different underglaze colors. Underglazes
are fantastic for creating designs and patterns that will show through the
glazed surface that you apply over them. Underglazes give the surface depth
and character, and an artist’s style can be amplified with the use of
underglazes on the clay surface. With so many different underglaze colors,
the design possibilities are practically endless!

Glazes

I use an assortment of commercially made glazes and mix larger batches of
some of the glazes I use the most. My classic white gloss glaze is one of
those examples. I use it on so many different pieces that I like to have a
larger batch of white at my disposal. Commercially made glazes are
available from all kinds of local and online ceramic supply retailers, and
they’re sold premixed in various-sized containers that range from small,
two-ounce (55 ml) jars, pint-sized (475 ml) containers, and even in one-
gallon (3.8 L) buckets.





    I love to shop for commercially made glazes because I don’t have access
to or room to properly store all of the raw materials that would be needed to
make as many different colors and textures of glazes that I like to use in my

work. Glazes are another material that should be properly stored and
labeled in your studio so that you know what you’re getting into and so that
glazes aren’t getting mixed up with each other. If you’re interested in
learning how to mix your own glazes, look for a course online or in person
where you live. There’s a lot of chemistry involved, and it’s a fairly
complicated process, but the results are really exciting, and it’s worth the
extra effort in a lot of ways. Commercially made glazes are just fine, and a
lot of professional ceramic artists proudly use these in their work. I’m
covering much more about glazes in chapter 2, so stay tuned!

Overglazes and Luster

If you can’t tell by looking at my work, gold luster is one of my favorite
ways to embellish and finish my creations. Overglazes and gold luster are
just as they sound. Gold luster is applied to the finished, vitrified glaze
surface with a fine-tipped brush in various patterns and designs and is fired
for the third time in the kiln. Luster is made from particles of real gold that
are suspended in a liquid medium, and it can be rather expensive. There are
a few different options for purchasing a gold luster. My preferred material is
the Premium Gold Luster from Duncan Ceramic Arts. It costs a little more
than the Bright Gold option, but the results are truly spectacular, and it’s
worth the extra money in my opinion! Lusters can be purchased from your
ceramics supplier, and they come in gold, silver, platinum, mother-of-pearl,
and even various colored lusters. I’ll explain how to use and apply gold
luster in chapter 2.
