         HOW TO USE THIS BOOK

The techniques and projects laid out in this book are intended to spark new ideas and
new directions for you to try out as you’re starting to discover the finishing process in
your own studio practice. I’m sharing just a small snapshot of my own approach when it
comes to what’s possible with surface design and finishing ceramics. The possibilities
really are unlimited, and I hope these projects and techniques can act as a jumping-off
point for you and your creative work. I want this book to inspire you as you start
discovering your unique artistic style and to serve as a reminder to embrace the process
and not just the outcome.

You should already have a basic understanding of the ceramics process as you start
approaching the techniques in this book. A lot of the projects I’m presenting and
demonstrating are starting from the middle stage—your work is already built and
you’re ready to start considering what the surface can be. Glazing and decorating your
ceramic creations is a fun step in the process, and I hope you’re inspired to dive in and
get started!

CHOOSING A CLAY BODY

There are a handful of things an artist needs to think about before they start
shopping around for clay. Some community pottery studios have
requirements on the types of clay you’re permitted to work with, but if the
options available to you feel endless and a little bit overwhelming, let’s
cover the main things to consider when choosing a clay body.
  TYPE OF CLAY: The differences in types of clay are primarily determined
by the different minerals making up the clay, the size of the platelets (thin
crystals) within the clay, the amount of plasticity (is the clay really sticky or
is it smooth and malleable?), and, of course, the firing temperature. The
three main types of clay that I would suggest for beginners are earthenware,
stoneware, and porcelain, but don’t let that stop you from trying out another
clay that you want to use.
  The type of clay you purchase is important to think about before getting
started because different kinds of clay work best for different projects. If
you’re making flower pots, a low-fire earthenware works great on the wheel
or with handbuilding, and it tends to be rather porous, so it’s good for
absorbing moisture. Earthenware is typically a red terra-cotta color, but you
can also find it in white. If you’re making a set of dinner plates, hearty
stoneware might be preferred as it’s a bit more chip- resistant than
earthenware. Stoneware clay can range in various shades of white, tan,
brown, red, black, and gray. A true porcelain clay body feels as smooth as
butter and is a lot less forgiving than other types of clay. If you really want
a challenge, try throwing with true porcelain on the wheel!

THE TEXTURE OF THE CLAY: Grog is that granular material within your
clay that kind of looks and feels like sand. This material, which is made
from ground-up fired clay, affects the building, throwing, and firing
properties of the clay. It’s good to know how much grog to expect in the
clay you’re purchasing because this adds some strength and workability to
your clay. There’s a range of grog in clay from fine to very coarse, and it
adds a distinct texture and feel to both wet clay and fully fired clay. Clay
with a heavily textured grog is great for handbuilding, while clay with fine
or minimal grog is ideal for throwing on the wheel.

FIRING TEMPERATURE (CONE SIZE) OF THE CLAY: A pyrometric cone reads
the temperature inside the kiln. These pyrometric cones are still widely used
today, although most kilns are computerized with digital readouts. These
cones were designed to melt and deform at the exact right time and
temperature to shut the kiln off at the precise moment. For the purposes of
finishing our ceramic works, it’s essential that the cone size of our clay
matches the cone size of our glazes. A low-fire clay goes with a low-fire
glaze, while a mid-range clay fits with a mid-range glaze, and so on.

COLOR OF THE CLAY: The color of the clay might be what first caught
your eye and makes you fall in love with something specific. Different
colors of clay provide different results, so let’s break down what to expect
with each one.

  WHITE: A white earthenware or a white porcelain clay body is your best
  choice if you want your vivid colors to pop. The colors tend to turn out
  the most vibrant when you’re working with a white clay body.
  TAN OR BUFF: This color is close to white, but it’s more like a sand or off-
  white tone. This clay is a fine choice for vivid, colorful finishings, and
   that soft sandy color won’t usually alter the colors of finished glazes.

RED: Red clay has such a deep, rich finish that I love. Red clay looks
   beautiful with matte, satin, or glossy glazes, and oftentimes, the clay is so
   beautiful that I don’t want to glaze it at all.
  BLACK: Get ready to fall in love! Black clay is one of my favorites. It
  looks beautiful all by itself without glaze, but finding a nice white glaze
  or underglaze makes a stunning contrast as well. Colors tend to get lost
  on a black clay body, so make sure you’re testing your glazes before
  committing to anything.
  MAKE YOUR OWN COLOR: Mason stain colorants can be added to your
  white clay to make a myriad of color-tinted clay. Finding the right
  amount of stain to mix and wedge into each clay body can vary from clay
   to clay, but blending your own clay colors is entirely possible and the
  colors can be left up to you.





  The main thing to keep in mind when choosing a clay body is to start by
working with a clay that you love the look of. Work with more than one

clay. Try as many clays as you want. While you’re starting out, all clay will
feel foreign to you, so you might as well start by picking one you like and
getting to know that clay. I have anywhere between five and eight different
clays going in my studio at any given point, so there’s no need to limit
yourself if a lot of different types of clay are calling to you. Throughout
most of this book, I’ll be working with stoneware, but you have the freedom
to pick what you like. Check with your nearest pottery supply shop to see
what’s available and don’t be afraid to ask questions! They’ll likely know
what direction to point you in.

ADDITIVE AND SUBTRACTIVE RELIEF DESIGNS

Sculptors and handbuilders typically
work in two different ways: additive
building and subtractive building.
The additive process involves
adding more clay and material to the
piece, changing its form and surface,
size, and proportions. The
subtractive process is all about
carving, where the clay is removed
and subtracted to reveal the form or
add dimension to the outer surface.
  When it comes to surface design
and decorating my pieces, I love to
make my pottery a little more sculptural by adding designs to the outer
surface with applied repeated shapes and textures. Additive elements can
change the surface and the form of the piece in a dramatic way.
  When you’re working in an additive process and focusing on the surface,
there are a few ways you can start.

If your clay is wet enough, coil building and additive sculpture work can
be as simple and easy as applying strips or pieces of clay in an even,
congruent pattern, without much scoring or slip to get the pieces to
adhere and join together. The added clay should be at the same stage of
wetness as the vessel so that the clay can continue drying and shrinking
at the same rate.
Another additive method is to cut and apply shapes to the surface in a
repeating pattern. This does require some scoring and slip to make the
connections, the clay attachments, and the clay vessel itself to be at the

same stage of drying and shrinking. If the attachments are drier than the
vessel they’re being fastened to, the clay will shrink at different rates and
likely crack at the connection.





Score and slip is the method of joining two pieces of clay together. It’s a
sound attachment technique for handles, sculptural pieces, or in our case,
the fusion of surface elements and details. There are a lot of different
methods and thoughts on how to properly mix and use a joining slip, so
you may want to research what technique works best for you. On my
wheel-thrown or handbuilt attachments, I use a slip made from my clay
shavings mixed with equal parts white vinegar and water. I don’t want it
to be too watery or too thick, and I usually mix a small amount of slip

each time I need to use it that is unique to whichever clay body I’m using
   that day.

   Subtractive surface design treatments look a lot like carving and textural
mark-making with various tools. I love including carvings and attachments
on the same piece to embrace both methods and give the piece more
dimension.

  When you’re starting to carve on the surface of your pieces, you really
  want to find the sweet spot when it comes to the state of drying. You
  don’t want your clay to be too wet as this makes carving much more
   difficult, and it can feel harder to control your hands and your tools. In
   contrast, you also don’t want your clay to be too dry as it’ll be very
   brittle, and you might crack the entire piece. I like to wait for the drying
  stage that comes right before the vessel is leather hard, when my tools
   slide through the clay just like butter. It’s important to keep close tabs on
   all of your studio projects so you don’t miss the right window of
  opportunity for certain steps.
   I prefer to build my carved pieces extra thick, as this gives me room to
  dig deep if I feel like it. If I’m making the base on a larger vessel, I’ll
  keep my slab at about a ⅝-inch (16 mm) thickness for deeper carvings. If
  I’m carving simple textures on the surface, I can keep the thickness of
  my walls at about ¼ inch (6 mm).

Larger, sculptural pieces with attachments and additive elements on the
surface require plenty of time to dry slowly. I like to keep recycled sheets of
plastic in the studio for wrapping pieces to aid in their slow drying.
Clothing covers from the dry cleaners are my favorite! I keep things tightly
wrapped in plastic for several days after I’m done building them. I check on
these pieces daily, and as they start to set up, I slowly unwrap the plastic
and let them begin to fully dry. Sometimes, the drying process can take a
couple of weeks, and it’s important not to rush this part.

UNDERSTANDING UNDERGLAZES

Underglazes are a really great starting point for pottery decoration. They’re
well suited for more intricate designs, they’re sometimes more forgiving
than glazes, and they act a lot more like acrylic paint than glaze when it
comes to final colors after firing and subtle layering. Underglazes can be
applied to leather-hard clay, to bisqueware, and carefully to dried
greenware, making it a very versatile material that’s able to be worked with
at different stages in the ceramics process. Underglazes can be purchased in
a variety of mediums: paint, crayon, pencil, watercolors, a stamp pad, or
pastel stick.





   Testing your underglazes on your preferred clay body is a good practice.
A test tile with the colors you’ve chosen will suffice. I start with two coats

of each color, labeled carefully next to each swatch as some of the
underglazes are similar in color or names to one another. I’ve also tested a
clear coat on each color swatch to get a sense of what each color looks like
when it’s sealed and glaze finished. Testing is always a good idea because
some colors turn out darker or different than you’d expect, so play around
with coverage and different mark-making in addition to the color swatch
tests. This will give you an idea of how the colors layer and how things
might look on a finished piece of pottery.





  You can apply underglazes in a lot of diverse ways to achieve different
effects. You can use paintbrushes in various shapes and sizes, or you can try
other things such as sponges, needle tools, or your fingertips—almost
anything can become a tool.

If I’m using a sponge or small-tipped tool for intricate textures, I only do
one stamp or drop of underglaze, knowing that I’m applying an adequate
amount of underglaze in that single coat.
If I’m painting the underglaze with a brush, I usually apply two to three
coats of the underglaze color because my brush has a tendency to pull
away or move some of the material I’m applying, so I’ll need another
coat to make sure I’ve achieved opaque coverage.

I typically seal my underglaze pieces with a clear coat of glaze,
especially if it’s a surface that’ll be used for food or drink or holding water,
like a vase. On sculptural pieces or planters, I like to leave some surface
area without a clear coat of glaze in order to embrace the matte surface
texture that the clay and the underglaze leave behind. It can be a lovely
contrast to the high-gloss clear coat.

GETTING TO KNOW YOUR GLAZES

A glaze is really just a layer of glass fused to the surface of ceramic. Glazes
are in a liquid state and can be applied to the bisque surface of a clay pot in
several different methods. When the liquid glaze is applied to bisqueware,
the water in the glaze is absorbed through the bisque surface and leaves
behind a dried powder layer. When fired at a very high temperature in the
kiln, it melts onto the surface of the clay. This glazed surface provides a seal
that is watertight, making it functional, hygienic, and decorative. Surface
decoration is my favorite step in the process and the whole focus of this
book. So, let’s dive right into glazing!

There are two ways to start when it comes to glazes. You can purchase
prepared and ready-to-use glazes from a pottery supplier, or you can mix
your own. If you’re a member of a community or school studio, you may
have access to large batches of shop glazes prepared in-house by a fellow
studio member. Making glazes from raw materials requires skill and
confidence and is a great area to explore if you’re ready to take a more
scientific approach for designing your surface. It allows for a wider range of
results and outcomes, and the process can be very rewarding when you’re
on a quest for a specific color or texture of glaze surface. There are several
glaze chemistry courses available, both online and in person, so if you’re
hoping to explore this area further, there’s a lot of information out there!

For the purpose of this book, I’ll be working mostly with commercial
glazes. Commercial glazes offer a very wide range of colors and textural
effects. These glazes are reliable, they tend to offer some consistency once
you’ve had the chance to get to know how they behave, and they’re great
for brushwork. A lot of commercial glazes come premixed in liquid form,
both in small jars and pints (475 ml) as well as gallon (950 ml) sizes. These
typically need a quick mix, shake, or stir and they’re ready to apply.
Commercial glazes can also be purchased in a dry powdered form. These
powdered glazes just need to be mixed with water and run through a sieve a
couple of times to break down the chunks of dried material. I’m proud to
use a lot of commercial glazes in my work! I also mix some of my own.
Both offer me what I’m looking for with color matching and textural
elements. The common thread here is devoting yourself to familiarity with
whatever glazes you choose to work with.
   Getting to know your glazes requires a lot of testing. And I mean a lot!
The true color and finish of a glaze won’t be revealed until it has been fully
fired and subjected to that intense heat within the kiln, which makes this
part of the process so exciting. It’s the reason why testing your glazes is so
important. You’ll be able to make more informed decisions on how to
decorate your ceramic work based on your testing experience and your
library of trusted results. As you advance your own skill set here, you’ll be
able to accurately predict your desired glaze results.

When testing your glazes, you’ll want to keep several things in mind as
you’re getting started. Here are some helpful glaze testing tips:

  Test glazes vertically as well as horizontally. This shows you how the
  glaze pools on a flat surface or if a glaze runs or drips down the vertical
   sides.
  Test your glazes on the clay you intend to use for your creations. If
  you’re using porcelain clay, test your glazes on that clay. If you’re also
  using stoneware clay, go ahead and test the same glazes on that clay too.
  There may be really interesting fluctuations between the different types
  of clay.
  Test tiles shouldn’t be too small. You want a large surface area as well as
  a partially textured surface so that you can see how the glaze behaves.
  This gives you enough surface area to gather ample information from
  your tests.

If you’re dipping your tests, dip it once halfway down the surface and
then dip it a second time all the way down the surface. You’ll see where
the double-dip overlaps to decide if one dip or two dips would be
preferred.

If you’re brushing your glazes, test what happens with one brushed coat,
two brushed coats, three brushed coats, and even four brushed coats. It’ll
help you determine how many brushed coats you want on your surface.
Keep detailed notes about your glaze tests. You’ll need a notebook for
note-taking as well as an underglaze pencil so that you can write notes
directly on the surface of your test tile. You’ll want to make labels for
everything you test. That way, you’ll know what’s what when it comes
out of the kiln.
Before and after example of 1, 2, 3, 4 coats of glaze, clockwise from top left.

Be methodical and create a labeling system for your glaze tests. Over
time, you’ll amass a large library of tests and information that’ll help you
design future works.
Understand that layering the glazes will also change your results. Red
layered on top of blue won’t necessarily create purple.





If your commercial glazes dry up, you can add more water and use an
emulsion blender to remix the glaze back to its original consistency.
Mixing sufficiently is the key here, so that your glazes don’t remain too
chunky.

I also like to use some of the dried pieces of glaze on the surface of flat
   pieces. I simply sprinkle it on top of a base glaze and let the kiln do the
   rest. This only works well if you have a flat surface to work on. I’ll be
  demonstrating this technique in the Drip and Splatter Platter project in
  chapter 4.

  Most importantly, remember that the foot of your piece or the bottom of
the pot, the part of the pot that comes in contact with the surface it’s sitting
upon, needs to be left completely unglazed. As the glaze turns to glass in
the kiln, it’ll fuse and stick to whatever surface it’s touching or applied to.
That means any drips or splashes of glaze need to be completely cleaned off
the foot of the vessel before it’s loaded into the kiln and onto the kiln

shelves. It also means that for the final firing, pieces should be loaded into
the kiln carefully, without touching any other pieces or the walls of the kiln.
Double-Checking to make sure your bottoms are sponged and cleaned is
essential!

APPLYING GLAZES

It’s best to apply your glaze to bisqueware that has been gently sponged off,
removing any dust or debris from the kiln or studio shelves. Some glazes
are suitable to be applied on raw, unfired clay, but throughout the book I’ll
only be demonstrating on bisqueware.

POURING GLAZES

  Pouring and dipping glazes are the quickest application methods. Pouring works great
   for overall coverage and single color works. The interior of a pot is usually poured, while
  the exterior is usually dipped.


STEP 1: Fill a cup or jar that’s about the same size as the vessel with glaze.
[A]

STEP 2: Pour the glaze inside the vessel, almost but not all the way to the
top. [B]

STEP 3: Quickly pour the glaze back out, giving the vessel a few spins so
that you can ensure the interior is fully coated in glaze. [C] This should be a
relatively quick motion.

STEP 4: Hold and carefully shake the vessel upside down until the liquid
glaze is poured all the way out. [D] You can use a paintbrush or sponge to
gently wipe away any drips.





    I wait for the poured glaze on the inside to fully dry before I dip or pour
or paint the outside. If the piece is too large to dip or if you only have a
small amount of glaze, you can pour the glaze on the outer surface of the
piece. This requires a committed movement without hesitation, so it’s best
to practice on something with lower stakes.

TO POUR THE EXTERIOR GLAZE, flip the piece upside down and place it on a
lift over a large bucket or dish to catch the excess poured glaze. Using a
measuring cup or a pint jar, pour the glaze over the exterior of the pot. One
pour should suffice if the entire surface has been covered.

DIPPING

Once you have poured the glaze on the interior of the pot, you can dip the exterior. If the
piece is a shallow plate, it’s possible to dip the piece entirely in one try. A more closed-off
opening, like a vase, should have the interior poured first and dipped second.
  Dipping can be done by hand or with dipping tongs. Some potters like to leave finger
marks where the piece was dipped, and others prefer a cleaner finish. Some pots have an
awkward grip or a low foot ring, and dipping tongs can offer a better grasp. Try both
methods and see which outcome you prefer.

Dipping with Tongs

Dipping tongs provide a secure hold for the fast dip motion. [A] [B]

Dipping by Hand

Hold the piece of pottery by the base [A] and plunge it vertically into the
glaze bucket. [B]

Like pouring, this technique requires a swift, quick motion—in and out.
[C] Then, hold the piece for a moment and wait for the glaze drips to drop
off. [D] Use a sponge to gently clean up any drips or any glaze that has
landed on the bottom of your piece.

The narrow opening creates a sort of vacuum and will prevent the glaze
from flooding the interior. [E] [F]

One dip should suffice but reference your glaze tests and notes to see if
any of your glazes prefer a double-dip. Some potters use a double- or a half-
dip as an aesthetic choice for finishing wares.

BRUSHING



Brushing is a great method for commercial glazes. It’s best for wide swaths
of color or patterns and not for small, detailed illustrations, although that
can work too. (Try using underglazes for more illustrative work.)
   Different glazes necessitate different brushstroke coverage. Some of the
glazes I use need only two solid brushed coats, while I like some glazes to
have four or more solid brushed coats.
   Finding the right brush is also a detail you won’t want to leave out.
Using your test methods, test some of your favorite glazes with assorted
paintbrushes and different stroke treatments. You’ll be surprised how much
variation there can be in opacity and texture. Small detail brushes are good
for little polka dots, while large brushes with soft bristles are great for more
gestural marks that drip and move a little bit.

Use tiles or test pieces of pottery for practicing your brushstroke mark-
making and determining how many coats of glaze you’ll need for your
preferred opacity and coverage.
  Pay attention to how far down on a vertical surface you apply the glaze.
If you know your glazes drip and run a little bit, leave extra space at the
bottom to allow for some of this movement to prevent your pot from getting
stuck to the kiln shelves because of a runny glaze.

SQUEEZING

  A small squeeze bottle can be used for making intricate glaze patterns, filling in shapes
  with glaze, or using various sizes of tips to trail the glaze in patterns or layering effects.
  This technique works best on flat works. Using a squeeze bottle on a vertical surface will
   likely lead to drips and your design running down the sides.


STEP 1: Start by filling a couple of small squeeze bottles with alternating
colors of glaze. [A] Using small test tiles, practice making shapes and lines
and different-sized dots and marks with your squeeze bottles. [B] Have fun
while you test out different patterns and layering effects. Let loose a little
bit!

STEP 2: Let the glaze fully dry before you try wiping the edges or making
notes on the bottom of the piece. Glaze trailing with squeeze bottles only
requires one even layer, as opposed to the multiple layers sometimes
required when brushing glazes on your wares.

OVERGLAZE AND LUSTER DECORATIONS

Gold luster quickly became something my work is known for. I fell in love
with using gold luster and the results it brought. It was intimidating to jump
right into using the material, but I’m the type of person that just needs to
dive in head first before I overanalyze what I’m up against. I plunged right
into overglaze gold application, and I still get excited each time I unload a
luster kiln.
   Metallic overglazes come in different types and finishes. Gold is the
most common and the one that I use the most. You can also find some
overglazes in white gold (a silver finish), bronze, and mother-of-pearl, as
well as other colored metallic overglazes. I don’t work with these others as
much. I prefer a gold finish with my work, so for the remainder of this
chapter, I’ll be talking mostly about my experience with gold luster.

Gold luster is an overglaze, meaning it’s applied over the vitrified,
glazed, and finished surface. The luster is made from real gold particles that
are suspended in a liquid medium. After it’s applied, it requires another
firing, and what’s left after this third firing is a layer of real melted gold on
the surface of your work. It’s a beautiful look and adds an incredible shine,
but it’s an intimidating process to dive right into, mostly because the gold
luster material is not cheap. It can be purchased in two forms: bright basic
gold luster and premium gold luster. I suggest using the bright gold when
you’re first starting out because it’s cheaper than the premium gold, but the
premium option is great for higher-end projects and it's what I’m using to
demonstrate. Gold luster comes in very small, two-gram bottles, but it’ll go

further than you think, especially if you’re just using the gold for small
accents.
    I use small detail brushes that are designed to be used with oil paints
when I’m working with luster. I like a rounded tip for my brush head, as it
makes spreading and moving the luster on the surface much easier. I keep
my luster brushes dedicated only to luster so as not to contaminate the
bristles with any other material. I clean my brushes in two easy steps and
have been using the same brushes for luster for several years, so it seems to
work just fine. To clean the brushes, I first dip and clean the bristles with
rubbing alcohol and then I clean them with dish soap and warm water and
dry them with a paper towel.

Luster has toxic fumes when in its liquid state, so safety is key. I feel
safest using this material in a well-ventilated space, with latex gloves and a
properly fitting respirator on my face. Beyond the safety requirements, I
really don’t like getting the luster on my skin, and I also don’t like the smell
of it. It stains my skin and my clothes if I happen to drip or smear some, so
I usually wear an apron along with the latex gloves while working with this
material. A fan and open windows or an open garage door can help air out
the space while you’re applying luster, or working outside when the
weather is nice is good too.
   Luster can be applied too thick, and it can be applied too thin. It’s a
finicky material as it likes things just right! If it’s applied too thick on a
vertical surface, it has a tendency to drip and run. Thicker areas of
application can have the occasional crack or bubble, but I think an
unintentional drip can look beautiful even if it’s not the desired result. If the

luster is applied too thin, it can look streaky, and instead of gold, it can have
reddish or purplish coloring in the streaky finish. If this happens, you can
refire the piece with another layer of gold on top. A smooth, even coverage
is what you’re aiming for when applying the gold luster. Slow, methodical
brushstrokes will serve you well. And as always, learn to embrace your
mistakes and roll with them. It makes for a great learning opportunity with
a new material, and so many people find subtle imperfections to be
charming and a big part of why handmade artwork is so treasured.
  Keep in mind that the gold luster takes on the finish and the surface
properties of whatever surface it’s applied to. So, if you’re adding luster to a
highly glossy surface, the gold will fire shiny and glossy as well. If you’re
adding the luster to a matte surface, the gold will fire in more of a matte
gold finish rather than a high-shine gold finish.

When it’s time to load the kiln, you can pack it tightly or loose,
depending on how many pieces you have to luster. (I always aim for a
tightly packed kiln for efficiency and no wasted space!) When you’re firing
your lustered pieces, it’s important to have your kiln isolated away from
your living or work area, as well as having the kiln appropriately ventilated.
Fumes are released into the air during firing, and you don’t want to breathe
that in. I fire gold luster to cone 018 in my kiln. This can be a fast firing,
usually two to three hours of firing and five to six hours of cooling. Some
people prefer to let their work sit for twenty-four hours after the application
of the gold and before firing. I don’t usually wait that twenty-four-hour
period and just load and fire the kiln immediately after I’ve applied the gold
on everything. I haven’t had any issues working this way, but you might
way to try other methods of waiting before firing, depending on the work
you’re making and the clay body you’re using.
  Keeping a clean workspace while using gold luster is also an important
part of the process, as well as keeping clean hands. If I smear the gold luster
I’ve just applied, it can leave a smudge or fingerprint after the firing.
Moving slowly and intentionally while I’m working is also important so
that I don’t spill my tiny bottle of gold luster. If you do make a mistake on a
glossy glazed surface, you can order something called a gold luster eraser.
This can help you remove any unwanted streaks or spots of gold, but it
doesn’t always work on all surfaces.

Gold luster is not dishwasher safe on finished work, and harsh soaps can
deteriorate the beautiful gold finish over time on lustered pieces. Also keep
in mind that this real gold finish is metallic, and it should never go in the
microwave. I have several gold luster mugs made by other artists in my
collection at home that I’ve always gently hand-washed over the years, and
everything has held up just fine!

INLAYING COLORED CLAY

Inlaying colored clay in slab form is just the combination of one colored
clay with another colored clay, right into the surface. It gives a beautiful
contrast and allows you to play around with different patterning within the
clay’s surface. You can purchase different colored clays, or you can use
stains to tint your own clay in various colors. Instead of tinting clay in
colors, I’m working with various clay bodies that all fire to the same
temperature and shrink at the same rate.





  When you’re combining different clay bodies, determining the shrinkage
rate on each clay body is key, as these clays need to shrink at a similar rate
and not clash with one another during drying or firing. To determine the
shrinkage rate of your clay, roll out a small slab of each of your different
clays. Using a ruler, trace a 5-inch (12.7 cm) line on the wet surface of each
slab with a needle tool. Label your clay samples and fire to the proper
temperature. If the two different clays have shrunk at the same rate,
meaning that the 5-inch (12.7 cm) lines you drew on each slab are the same
size, then they should be compatible when combined.

An off-white stoneware with speckles is my base clay, and bright white
stoneware or black stoneware is used for my patterned inlaid pieces. I start
by rolling a slab for my inlaid pieces. I roll out a slab of white stoneware to
a ⅛-inch (3 mm) thickness. I cut out my shapes or inlaid pieces smaller than
what I’m expecting the final pattern to be, knowing that these will get rolled
and stretched out as they’re being pressed into the base clay. Once I’ve cut
my shapes from my ⅛-inch (6 mm) thick inlay slab, I cover those cutouts in
plastic and set them aside.

Now, I can start rolling my base slab, rotating and flipping directionally
so that it doesn’t get rolled out too narrow or too long for the shape of the
piece I’m making. I stop rolling when my slab is about 1 inch (2.5 cm)
thick. This is when I start to lay out my pattern of cut pieces. Your inlaid
shapes can be organic and irregular, or you can build a more structured
pattern like I am, with checkered squares. Once your pattern is laid out on
the top surface, you can roll the slab back out to a 1-inch (2.5 cm)
thickness. This gets the pattern pressed in on its first roll. As you start to get
the slab rolled out thinner, you can start rotating the slab so that your inlaid
pattern gets stretched evenly in all directions. Stop rolling when your slab is

¼ inch (6 mm) thick. I think ¼ inch (6 mm) is a great thickness for slab-
built plates and trays, but feel free to go a bit thinner if you like.
    I then use my silicone rib tool to compress and smooth the inlaid pattern
in all directions. Compressing is great for getting rid of unwanted finger
marks or canvas texture, but it also helps strengthen the platelets of the clay
so that the two clays are firmly inlaid together.

TROUBLESHOOTING
. . . and What to Do When Things Don’t Go as Planned

When it comes to finishing our ceramic creations, the finality of these
choices can sometimes feel like a major hang-up when we’re trying to
decide on a direction or a style to embrace. Part of the ceramics process is
learning when to relinquish some control and leave our expectations open to
whatever happens. A lot of times, we find results that really excite us and
inspire new ideas and creative directions, but it’s always a letdown when
things don’t go as planned and we’re unhappy with the results.

Not everything can be saved, but some situations can handle another
layer of glaze or another round in the kiln. Here are some tips if you have a
piece that might want another touch-up:

  REFIRING: Some ceramics will accept another layer of glaze after being
   fully glaze fired. You have the opportunity to add another layer of glaze
  on top of your piece and to fire it again. This can be helpful if you have
   blisters or bubbles in the glaze’s surface or a streaky side that didn’t get
  enough glaze coverage when you first glazed it. It doesn’t always make a
   drastic change, but it can even out some of your coverage if you’re
  working with a solid color. You can also do this with gold luster. If
   there’s an area that didn’t get enough luster and looks a bit streaky, you
  can add another layer with your fine-tip brush and fire it again.

CRACKS: Cracks in finished work can be a total drag, and there’s not
much you can do to salvage it. But cracks within your bisqueware can be
patched and mended with a material called Bisque Fix if you just can’t let
it go. It’s a white paste that can be applied with a paintbrush to fill the
cracks. Once it’s applied to the cracked area, you can smooth it out with a
sponge or lightly sand with a piece of sandpaper. Then, go ahead and
glaze the piece of bisqueware as you normally would and fire to the
proper temperature. Bisque Fix comes in white, so it won’t blend in
perfectly with all clay bodies, but it can be colored with ceramic stain or
metal oxides. It adheres securely to the bisqueware and patches things
watertight. Embrace the imperfections and let your creations live on!

GLAZE STUCK TO KILN SHELVES AND POTS STUCK TO KILN SHELVES: A
glaze drip or a glaze that runs is not uncommon in a ceramics studio, and
we’ve all had a pot or two that ends up fused to the kiln shelf on account
of a runny glaze. There’s not always something that can fix the pot in this
situation, but you can usually salvage your kiln shelves. Some pots need
to be broken off of the shelf and scraped away, while some will pop right
off but leave behind broken chips of glass glaze where the pot was stuck.
If you’re trying to keep things out of the trash, you can don some safety
goggles and use a Dremel multitool to grind the jagged broken parts off
so that they aren’t so sharp. Always use tools like this with the utmost
care and safety. Chips of glaze act in the same way as glass, and even the
smallest piece can cut you just like a tiny shard of glass would.

Testing is the key to catching issues before they end up on the surface of
your pots. Some of my clays will reject certain underglazes or glazes that
work fine on my other clays. They blister and bubble or flake off the
surface of the clay during firing. This is precisely why you want to test
things over and over again.

        PLANNING YOUR SURFACE DESIGN

As an artist, I pour a lot of my feelings and my emotions into the process, resulting in an
artistic expression that reflects my personality in the form of my style and my
inclinations. This is the intuitive approach that more than fifteen years of experience in
ceramics has taught me. Mark-making and shape construction can occur spontaneously
the more I explore with tools or materials throughout the creation process, but deep
within me, I’m deciding on what is exciting and beautiful without consciously knowing
why. I’ve worked many hours in my studio and in my creative practice to get to a place of
intuitive creation.

THE INTELLECTUAL APPROACH

Alternatively, as artists and creative beings, we can create by using a more
intellectual approach, which is what this section is all about. As artists, we
get to present our own view of the world, but sometimes a solution needs to
be found, a problem needs to be solved, a goal needs to be met, and a new
way of working needs to be prioritized. We figure out what the goals of the
project are and what limitations we face, and we analyze all of the options
available. Changes are likely made along the way, and the process is
repeated again and again. This way of creating requires more systematic
thinking to sort out the possibilities and articulate the visual decisions.
Designers employ these methods all the time when solving problems for
clients, and artists can use these same principles to articulate their creative
vision.





   In this section, I’m highlighting my top five design principles to consider
when getting started decorating your own pottery and making more

informed decisions about ceramic surface design. Those five principles are
Form, Color, Pattern, Texture, and Function.

FORM

Even though this book is primarily focused on surface design and
decoration, the form of your work needs to be thoughtfully considered.
Form is always a good place to start as we want to know what kind of
object we’ll be creating. I usually start with my sketchbook, where shapes
and silhouettes start to fill my page, and I begin drawing what I find
interesting and beautiful. This stage of my process feels very explorative
and fluid, and I find that I’m responding more to certain iterations of form
than to others, and that clues me in on a direction to start traveling in.
  Most of the forms that make it out of my sketchbook and into clay are
simple ones. I like to work on flat surfaces and very simple, plain, three-
dimensional forms. I embrace simple shapes because my emphasis is
typically on color and pattern and glaze movement within the surface. I
treat these forms as blank canvases (some feeling quite literally like
canvases) and start to notice repetition and different iterations on cylindrical
and bottle forms, rounded spherical forms, flat organic tiles cut into various
sizes and shapes, and many shapes of plates, trays, platters, and dishes.
These straightforward shapes and simple forms have become part of my
repertoire, and I catch myself repeating them and altering them in classic
production potter practice.

But the artist inside of me has a strong desire to create more one-of-a-
kind forms, and in the early handbuilding stages is where I let myself have a
little more fun with the form I’m building. I start with adding feet, a
decorative rim, or additive sculptural elements until the basic form has
morphed into something more interesting and unique. Sometimes, it’s a
matter of combining two or more forms to create something new. Take, for
instance, the bottle form as a vase. I can do a lot of different things while
I’m building the form and to the surface as I’m finishing the vase to make
each one feel different, even when the underlying form is basically the
same.
  When planning your own forms, use these beginning stages to determine
what kind of clay you’ll use, what coloring and patterning techniques you’ll
use, and how you’ll finish the work. Ceramic forms require some
preplanning, and you’ll find yourself considering the things that you can’t
see yet in the early prototyping stages. You can also let the objects take on
their own form as you build and as you work. It doesn’t have to be fixed
and final. The techniques you adopt over time will change. You’ll begin to
discover new materials, you’ll develop new techniques, and naturally, the
forms you create will start to evolve. The form should always be considered

in functional work and nonfunctional work, and over time, as you refine
and improve your skills, you’ll be better able to carry out your early
intentions when building new forms in the studio.
  As a quick note to keep in mind, a shape is two-dimensional, like an
outline or a silhouette. It has height and width. The form is three-
dimensional. It has height, width, and depth. Plan your forms, research
other forms, sketch and test out your own ideas, build prototypes, and return
to old forms and rethink them. Repeat over and over until you’ve got the
hang of it. Challenge yourself to create a form you’ve never seen before!

COLOR

Color within ceramics can be achieved in so many different ways and at so
many various stages throughout the process. At the very start, the clay
we’re working with presents a certain color on its own, and the possible
variations in glaze finishes and color combinations available to us are
nearly endless. Color can but doesn’t have to play a big role in the finishing
of ceramics.
  When you think about what you want to build, do you see it with an
earthy, neutral-toned palette or more vibrant with bright pops of color?
Right from the start, you’ll want to choose your clay with this in mind. A
white stoneware clay accepts color differently than a dark brown or black
stoneware clay. Then, when it’s time to pick colors for the finished surface
of your pieces, you’ll have to decide which colors are complementary
together. These steps take planning and a bit of strategic thinking even at
the earliest stages.

I work at both ends of the color spectrum. I have some pieces that
include several different colors all on the same piece and some that
highlight the neutral tones and earthiness of the raw clay without much
color at all. Both excite me and are ever-present throughout my work and
still feel like my style even when the colors I’ve used vary greatly.
   Start by building a glaze library full of the tests of specific colors that
interest you most. Test those glazes on all your different clay bodies and
find out what changes and what you like the most. You’ll start spending
more time with those glazes and analyzing their results on various clay
bodies in varied layers and application techniques to determine which
colors and finishes are working and which aren’t.

PATTERN

Patterns are created when shapes, lines, colors, and other elements are
repeated at regular intervals throughout the surface of the pot. Negative
space and positive space can both aid in building patterns, and the
continuation of the pattern carries the viewer’s eye smoothly from one point
to the next. Patterns can be very simple or more stylized and intricate. A
strong pattern has the ability to unify the surface of your pots with the pot
itself. A lot of classic patterns, like stripes and polka dots, can be worked
with in unique and innovative ways that really bring your ceramic surfaces
to life, and patterns don’t have to be repeated constantly. You can still
achieve unity in your finished designs with a bit of variety.
   There are so many different ways to enhance your handbuilt and wheel-
thrown ceramic works through the use of patterns. A pattern can be worked
into your designs at any stage of creation in the ceramics process. You can
use carving techniques or additive sculptural elements to the outer surface
of your moist clay creations in various patterns on your piece. These added
or subtracted elements bring a base level of patterning directly into your
clay work, and the handiwork is impressive on its own or with added
elements of color and texture.
  Once your work is dried and bisque fired, you can start to use vibrant
and colorful underglazes and glazes to add unique patterns and designs to
the surface of your pots. Application methods for creating patterns vary just
as widely as the patterns do themselves.

If you’re stumped with how to get started working with patterns, try
taking some time with your sketchbook. Get inspired by nature, take a stroll
through your local library, or go to an art museum or a local clothing store
and take note of all the patterns you find out in the wild. They’re
everywhere once you start looking for them! A sketchbook filled with small
samples of patterns makes a nice starting point when you’re stuck at the
studio in need of some inspiration.
   Life is not always orderly, and neither is ceramics. Oftentimes, surprises
and the unexpected can force your creative plans to shift while working. As
an artist, I’ve purposely chosen to offset the unifying aspects of my work
and let some of the elements appear. As uncontrollable as this can feel, it
frees me of normal design restraints. I love sticking to a rhythm and a
predictable pattern, but I also love it when my materials show me the way.

TEXTURE

Texture can be achieved at all stages of the creation process in ceramics,
and it’s one of my favorite ways to make a statement with the surface of my
work. Starting at the earliest stages, simple and complex carving can be
done with tools, stamps, and found objects pressed into the clay’s surface,
and additive, attached designs are all great ways to create dimensional
texture at the beginning stage of creation. Underglaze and various glazes
can offer textural finishes at the bisque stage of pottery decoration, giving
you endless opportunities to embellish and highlight the surface of your
pottery or sculpture. Even the type of clay you choose to work with plays a
big part in the texture of your finished piece. Clays containing more grog,
like a stoneware clay, will fire and finish with a rough, earthy, speckled
texture, while clays like porcelain will finish with a brighter, smoother-
textured surface.





  As an avid handbuilder, I sometimes embrace and leave behind the
simple finger marks my hands have left in the clay’s surface. Instead of
trying to completely smooth the surface of the piece, the marks of the
maker are intentionally left behind and become part of the piece’s surface
texture. Most people love this aspect of handmade work. Texture in the
clay’s surface can be part of the direction of the design of the piece, and

carving is a great way to achieve this. This relief carving can be
accomplished with varying sizes and shapes of carving tools in repetitive
strokes, organic lines, and free-flowing marks taken away from the clay’s
surface, creating a uniquely tactile finish.
  On the flip side, we can also use an additive process where we create
texture by adding clay to the surface of the pot in an effort to create more
dimensional exterior texture. This can be easiest at the early stages of
building when the clay is most willing to be manipulated. It can also be
achieved through the design and use of attachments added to the surface. I
like to use simple shapes that I attach to the exterior surface of the piece in
an all-over pattern as a way of creating a simple, but stylized, decorative
vessel. This process is great for planters and other decorative vessels that
serve the function of beauty, but won’t necessarily be handled and used on a
daily basis.

  The opportunity to add texture to the surface of your work by utilizing
glazes is beloved by many ceramic artists and cannot be forgotten when
talking about texture. It goes without saying that many glazes offer varying
textures of finish, such as matte, glossy, and satin. All of these finishes
provide a different texture and tactile feel to the pot’s surface. Some glazes
will crawl and craze and crackle, and that finish provides a distinct look and
feel on the surface of our pots. We can even create textural finishes by
layering our glazes. Overlaying one glaze onto another gives a different
result than the two glazes do on their own. Using this to our advantage, we
can practice layering our glazes to achieve different finishes and effects.
When applied generously, the glazes can drip and layer upon themselves,
creating even more textural surface effects.

FUNCTION

I got into pottery because I loved making pieces that I could use and live
with on a daily basis. It just made sense in my mind to make functional
pottery pieces that I could drink from, eat off of, and plant houseplants in.
As I started developing my style and my creative voice, I started creating
objects that barely served a function, while some things served very strange
and specific functions. Making art and making functional objects go hand in
hand for me. They both inform the other and allow me the opportunity to
express my ideas but without the pressure of making something useful all of
the time.
  You can create pieces of art that serve no purpose, and you can also
create pieces of art that serve a very specific purpose. I like to create both.
As you’re starting out, ask yourself, “What is the desired function of this
new piece?” There are so many different factors to include when you’re
creating and designing something new.





    If you’re making a ceramic coffee mug, for instance, there are certain
things to consider in relation to how the mug will function. Does the handle
feel good in your hand as it’s being held? Does the rim of the mug feel nice
as it touches your lips and you take a sip? Does the foot sit firmly on the
table so the mug doesn’t tip over or wobble too easily? These are all things

to consider as you’re working through each stage of designing and creating
functional work because all parts need to be thoughtfully considered.
   Just keep in mind that all your creations do not need to be functional.
Create art just for the fun of it! Sculptures, wall art, figurative work, and
self-portraits are important and necessary in our lives and our homes. So are
cups and scoops and plates. Find out what your desired function is when
you’re starting your own creations and embrace whatever direction your
creative intuition takes you in.

KEEPING A SKETCHBOOK

A sketchbook is the perfect creative companion for getting our thoughts and
ideas down on paper. I carry my sketchbook with me everywhere I go
because I truly never know when inspiration will hit, and it’s a great way to
pass time when I’m waiting around for something. I use my sketchbook to
plan the forms I’ll build in the studio and for planning the marks and
patterns I’ll embrace on the surface of my work. It has also become a
glorified coloring book for when I just want to calm my mind and keep my
hands busy. I test out a lot of different color combinations to find out which
colors look great next to one another, and I use those pages as a starting
point when I’m bringing my creative ideas to life.
  Your sketchbook can be used for notes to yourself or tiny taped pieces of
found paper inspiration for your future self. It can be a private space for
creative expansion or something you turn into art that gets shared with
those around you. When you use your sketchbook regularly, it can lead to
creative breakthroughs and unlock brand new ideas for creative projects
you want to start in the studio. A sketchbook is also very useful for relaxing
and clearing your mind because we all can benefit from sitting down to just
draw and color sometimes. It’s a useful tool that can help you keep your
creative inner flame burning bright.

           IDEAS FOR GETTING STARTED

The time has come to dive in and get started! Are you ready? Where will you begin? My
hope is that these projects will spark ideas that inspire you to take new directions in
