SET OF COASTERS

It’s been a personal goal of mine to make more things just for fun and just for me. As a
full-time potter, I spend most of my time in the studio producing work for other people. I
love my job, and I love creating artwork that lives in the homes and the worlds of other
people. Somewhere along the way, I forgot the joys and pleasures of crafting something
special for my own personal gratification. A set of ceramic coasters became that
household object that I knew was missing in my life.
   Living with art every day can be as simple as a handmade set of coasters on your
coffee table or your nightstand. A coaster is practical and functional, and I think it might
as well be beautiful too. Coasters can be used in every room of the house, on any surface
area where you’d set a glass of water or an ice-cold beverage. They help protect your
household surfaces by preventing any ring marks caused by cups and mugs of your
various refreshments.
  When you’re starting your own set of coasters, take the opportunity to play around
with pattern and color. Working on a flat surface that won’t be used for serving food
means you can experiment with different glaze textures as well as intricate, colorful
designs. You have lots of opportunities to explore various shapes of coasters too. I went
with the classic circle and square coasters for the set I’m making, but you can go wild
with unique organic shapes if you like. Let’s get started!



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

Bisque-fired ceramic coasters (My circles are approximately 4 inches [10 cm] in
  diameter; my squares are approximately 4 inches [10 cm] square)
Sponge
Bucket of water
Pencil and ruler
Various glazes
Assorted paintbrushes, including fine tip and flat head, for applying glazes
Squeeze bottles with assorted tip sizes for applying glazes
Optional: underglaze pencil or pottery stamp

Instructions

STEP 1 Gently wipe clean any dust or debris from your bisque-fired ceramic
coasters. Using your pencil, start sketching out the design or pattern you’re
envisioning for the surface of your coasters. [A] [B] [C]

STEP 2 Using various fine-tip paintbrushes, start filling in your patterns on
the surface of the coaster with glaze. [D] If you’re brushing your glaze, it’s
important to make sure you’re applying multiple coats of glaze on each
section of the pattern, focusing on even coverage throughout the whole
surface. [E] Since you’ve already spent time experimenting with your glaze
testing, you should already know how many coats you need for each glaze
to achieve the desired finish.

STEP 3 Using a small squeeze bottle is a quicker option since it only requires
one layer of glaze application, but it does require more controlled
movements and careful pressure so as not to release too much glaze and
mess up the pattern. Go slow and fill in your shapes and patterns following
the pencil lines as your guide. [F] Let the glazes dry in between coats and
when switching glaze colors.

STEP 4 Once you’ve finished your glaze layers and patterns, use a damp
sponge to clean the edges and wipe off any drips of glaze on the underside
of the coaster too. Let the glazes dry, then sign your name or stamp your
logo and set each coaster aside for firing.

BEADS

I have very busy hands! I like it best when I’m making things in the studio, but
sometimes, simple activities at home can do the trick too. Whether it’s cooking, washing
dishes, pulling weeds in the garden, or mending a piece of clothing, I like having a
creative task for my hands. As it turns out, having occupied hands is very good for the
brain and aids in stronger mental health. The handiwork is present in all stages of bead
making—from rolling the wet clay into small shapes and spheres to glazing small
designs and patterns on the beads and then stringing up your finished beads into
something unique. The palpable reward is there at each phase of the process.
  When you’re making your beads out of clay, don’t forget to use a needle tool or a
bamboo skewer to poke a hole through the center. The hole needs to be big enough so
that your bead will fit onto the bead rack you’re using during firing, as well as fitting onto
the cord you plan on using to string the beads, so keep shrinkage in mind as you’re
working on your beads.
   “What’s a bead rack,” you ask? It’s a kiln-safe rack with high-temperature rods that the
glazed beads are threaded onto for firing. It suspends the beads in mid-air so that you can
have a glaze all the way around the bead, without having it get stuck to the kiln shelf
during the glaze firing. Remember that glaze will fuse to whatever surface it touches in
the kiln, so it is important that the inner channel of the bead stays clean and free from
any glaze drips. Otherwise it will fuse itself to the bead rack and be stuck. You’ll only need
to use the bead rack for the glaze firing stage, not for the bisque firing stage.
  Handmade ceramic beads have such a tactile quality to them that just can’t compare
to store-bought plastic beads. Ceramic beads can be used for necklaces, longer wall
garlands, small key chains, ornaments, and the like, and making them offers a therapeutic
way to pass the time, giving your hands something creative to do to stay busy.



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

Clay for rolling and making the beads and a needle tool or bamboo skewer for poking
  holes in the beads or prepared bisque-fired ceramic beads (any shape and size)
Sponge
Bucket of water
Various glazes
Assorted paintbrushes, including small detail brushes, for applying glazes
Bead rack for glaze firing
Cord for stringing beads

Instructions

STEP 1 Once you’ve determined what you want to create using your finished
beads, start making your beads with clay. If you’re making a necklace with
beads that match, make the beads about the same size using the same clay
so that they string up nicely. If you’re like me, and you love a bowl full of
mismatched beads, make them as unique and funky as you’d like! Don’t
forget to make the hole big enough so the beads fit on the firing rack (if
you’re glazing them) and on the string or cord you’re using for your
finished creation. [A] [B]

STEP 2 Allow your beads to dry completely. Refine them with a damp
sponge and prepare for bisque firing. I like to fire my beads inside of a cup
or a bowl so that they don’t roll off my kiln shelves. [C]

STEP 3 Once you have bisque-fired beads, you can start thinking about color
and patterns and how you want to glaze your beads. I like to use a fine-tip
brush for layering in stripes or small polka dots or layered shapes. [D]





Beads are an excellent surface for playing with layering and texture, so feel
free to get adventurous. Be sure to keep the inner channel of the beads clean
and free from any glaze drips or smears. Glaze on the inside of the beads
will cause them to get stuck to the high-temperature rod of the bead rack
during firing.

STEP 4 Once your beads are glazed, carefully clean them and slowly start to
fill the rods with beads one at a time, allowing ample room in between to
make sure that the beads don’t touch. [E] I use my bead rack at the top layer
of my kiln load. It’s much easier to fill and load this way if it’s near the top
instead of the bottom. Assemble the rack pieces first and then add each
filled firing rod one at a time to the rack. Once it’s loaded in the kiln,
double-check your spacing to make sure each bead has enough room and
isn’t touching the bead next to it or the rack itself. If you don’t want to
glaze your beads and prefer to keep the surface of the clay bead raw, you
can fire your beads directly on the kiln shelf instead, without the bead rack.
Fire to the proper temperature and let cool slowly.

STEP 5 When the kiln is cool enough to be unloaded, carefully disassemble
the bead rack one rod at a time. [F] Some of the beads will slip off easily,
and some of the beads will take some wiggling to pry loose. If your bead
gets stuck, you can break the bead off of the rod or use a pair of pliers to try
to force the bead off. Make sure you don’t have any sharp bits of glaze
sticking off the surface of your beads.
STEP 6 String up your beads and build your creation! [G]

SPOONS

A ceramic scoop or spoon can be a sweet little project for all kinds of uses. I like to make a
long skinny handled spoon as a cocktail stirrer. I also like making a small handheld scoop
for coffee beans or coffee grounds. A tiny spoon is a great sidekick to a small vessel for
sprinkling sea salt. The sky is the limit for all the ways a handmade spoon can be used.
  Because of their small size, these pieces will sit directly on the kiln shelves, so I have to
be careful where I add glaze. I like using underglaze designs for finishing my spoons so
that I don’t have to worry about any glazed surfaces laying against the kiln shelves. On
my spoons and scoops, the entire underside is left without glaze, and the spoons
sometimes just have the spoon head glazed and nothing else. If my spoon is little, I make
a hole at the end of the handle and slide it onto my bead rack for firing. This allows me to
glaze the entire surface of the spoon if that’s the finished look I’m going for. Keep in mind
that the spoon has to be small enough to be able to hang from the bead rack in the kiln
without touching the shelves.



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

Clay for handbuilding your spoons or finished bisque-fired ceramic spoons and scoops
  in various sizes and shapes
Sponge
Bucket of water
Various lead-free, nontoxic, food-safe glazes (underglazes and clear glaze)
Assorted paintbrushes, including small detail brushes, for applying glazes
Optional: bead rack

Instructions

STEP 1 Start by handbuilding your spoons. Which clay will you use? How
big will they be? Will you hang them from a bead rack or fire them directly
on the kiln shelves? These are important questions to ask yourself before
you begin to determine your design direction. A modest rounded spoon
head attached to a handle works great as a simple starting point. [A]

STEP 2 After bisque firing and gently sponging off my spoon, I start adding
my colorful underglaze stripes. [B] I’m applying three coats of underglaze
with small detail brushes so I can make my lines extra skinny. I’m making
thinner lines so I can fit more colors on the spoon, but I could change my
line thickness for more of a color-block look instead. This is where pattern
work and layering can be really interesting with your underglaze colors.
Repeat your three-coat coverage with each color.

STEP 3 Once I’ve finished my underglaze decoration, I let the colors dry
completely before I handle it too much and mess up my designs. I apply
three coats of a clear glaze on the head of the spoon, sponge off the edges
and the underside of the spoon for any glaze drips, and prepare my spoon
for firing. [C]





STEP 4 After your spoon is fired, gently clean it, and it’s ready to use! I like
to use my spoons for sea salt and spices in the kitchen, but they also make
lovely decorative objects when displayed on a small shelf of various
collectibles.

WALL HANGINGS

Ceramic wall hangings have always been one of my favorite things to glaze when I’m
working in the studio. They allow me an opportunity to be spontaneous with my color
choices and get some funky shapes and textures in there that aren’t always suitable for
functional pieces. I like to emphasize the beauty of the raw texture of my clay in a lot of
these wall hangings. The dot pattern has become one of my go-to designs, and I love
when each wall hanging turns out one of a kind.
    I build wall hangings in all different shapes and sizes. I like to make irregular shapes
because I always have a small wall area in my home that needs a unique piece of artwork
—a narrow strip of wall where a framed painting or photograph won’t quite fit. I like
emphasizing the imperfect, torn edges on some. While certain wall hangings call for a
smooth and sharp rectangular or square shape, others have rounded corners. This body
of work really allows me to play with my materials and try new things. Those kinds of
projects are so beneficial to a creative mind!
  While you’re building your slabs from clay, there are a few things you want to
remember. Drying your slabs slowly and strategically so that they dry flat and aren’t
warped is ideal. Having a flat wall hanging means it’ll hang flush against the wall. And
don’t forget to include a hole toward the top so you can hang it up. If you do forget the
hang hole, I also like to set these pieces on a shelf and lean them against the wall. They’re
versatile and can add a unique pop of art and color to your home in almost any fickle spot.
  Ceramic wall hangings are a fun way to express yourself with a more painterly
approach to glazing. You can use a project like this to play around with patterns and
mark-making, as well as different brushing and squeeze-bottle glaze techniques. It’s a
flat, blank canvas ready for your artistic touch!



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

Flat, fired bisqueware, designed to hang on or lean against a wall
Sponge
Bucket of water
Pencil, ruler, and stencils or paper templates for tracing your designs
Various glazes
Assorted paintbrushes for applying glazes
Squeeze bottles with assorted tip sizes for applying glazes
Optional: underglaze pencil

Instructions

STEP 1 Gently wipe clean your bisqueware with a damp sponge. Start
sketching or tracing your designs directly onto your flat, bisque-fired wall
pieces. Lead pencil marks will burn off in the kiln when they are fired, so
don’t stress if you change your patterns or make a mark in the wrong place.
[A]

STEP 2 Start choosing your glazes. [B] Some of my wall hangings have up to
twelve different glazes on them, so don’t be shy with your glaze choices.
Go with what feels right. [C]

STEP 3 When you start painting or squeezing your glazes onto your designs,
keep in mind that the color of the liquid glaze will look totally different in
its current state than it will when it’s fully fired. [D] [E] So, you’ll have to
rely on your extensive glaze-testing knowledge, your sample library, your
glaze notes, and your sketchbook so that you can properly anticipate the
final results ahead of time. It’s a little bit like thinking and working
backward—you’re working with materials that will look different at the
end, and sometimes it’s challenging to paint using just your imagination.

STEP 4 Once you’ve finished painting your wall hanging, use your damp
sponge to clean up the edges, wipe off the back side, and clean up any drips
or smears.

STEP 5 If you want, use an underglaze pencil to sign your name on the back.
Be careful not to smudge the freshly written signature or flake off any of the
glazes on the front. This piece is delicate at all stages, so handle it slowly
and load it into the kiln carefully.

STEP 6 Once it’s been fully fired, proudly display your piece and admire
your handiwork. Either hang it up with a nail or a screw, [F] making sure it
has a solid hold, or position it prominently on a shelf or mantle, propped up
against the wall.

ABSTRACT CHEESEBOARDS

I’m a big fan of a well-rounded snack dinner, and I’ve become very good at building a
proper cheeseboard. Whether it’s for myself or a group of friends I’m entertaining at my
place, I like to lay out a fabulous spread of cheeses on a beautiful cheeseboard because it’s
as much fun to focus on the presentation as it is to eat it.
   Starting from the wet clay stage, I’ve built my cheeseboards thicker than my wall
hangings because I want them to be used for serving and a thicker final slab feels more
durable for picking up and passing around the table. I’ve made a bigger hole at the top so
that my finger can rest in there when I’m holding it or passing it, and it can also be hung
on the wall in the kitchen when it’s not in use. An abstract, all-over pattern turns your
board into a lovely eye-catching piece of art when it’s not covered in fruit and cheese!
   Since this project idea is embracing a functional serving piece, it’s necessary to use
lead-free, nontoxic, food-safe glaze. Unlike artwork intended for wall hangings, we want
to avoid heavily textured glazes or surfaces that are too porous for this project. Think
about what will come into contact with that surface—hard and soft cheeses, fruit, and
utensils. A high-gloss glaze will feel different from a matte finish, so think about this as
you pick your glazes. You’ll also want to think about ease of cleanup and how a cheese
knife will behave when it brushes against the surface of the glaze.



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

Bisqueware ready for glaze
Pencil, ruler, and stencils or paper templates for tracing your designs
Various lead-free, nontoxic, food-safe glazes
Assorted paintbrushes, squeeze bottles, and other glaze application tools
Sponge
Bucket of water

Instructions

STEP 1 Using a pencil, draw out your design or pattern on your bisque-fired
surface. You can trace objects or stencils for varying shapes on the surface
or fill it out with an allover pattern. [A] Decide if you want the surface fully
covered or if you want any raw clay showing around the edge of your
designs.

STEP 2 Start with your first glaze color and begin filling in your shapes or
patterns. [B] If you’re using squeeze bottles, you can do one pass of glaze. If
you’re brushing it on, don’t forget to think about how many layers you’ll
need for full glaze coverage.

STEP 3 Alternate your colors and your glaze choices as you start to fill in
your patterns and designs. [C] [D] Once it feels complete, clean up and
prepare your piece for firing. [E]
STEP 4 Once it’s fired and ready to use, it’s time for a snack party! [F]

SET OF CUPS

Ceramic mugs and tumblers are the “best sellers” when it comes to my studio inventory,
and I can barely keep enough of them in stock. I think it’s because everyone knows
exactly what to do with a cup or a mug, and whatever our preferred beverage is, a special
cup is a great way to elevate a daily routine.
  One of the most important things to remember when you’re glazing cups or any other
vertical ceramic work is to test your glazes on upright surfaces as well as flat surfaces so
that you know which glazes tend to run and which ones are stable. You want to avoid
glazes that will trickle down the surface and cause your vessel to get stuck to the kiln
shelf during firing.
    I like to leave a lot of the clay surface exposed on my cups and mugs because I have so
many different clay bodies that are just too beautiful to cover up. For this project
example, I’m using deep red stoneware, and I’ll be leaving some of the exterior surfaces
unglazed so that the beauty of the clay really shows through.



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

Bisque-fired cups or mugs (I’m making a set of four matching mugs)
Sponge
Bucket of water
Various lead-free, nontoxic, food-safe glazes (I’ll be using 6 to 8 different glazes on this
  project)
Assorted paintbrushes for applying glazes

Instructions

STEP 1 Wipe clean the inner and outer surfaces with a damp sponge,
removing any dust or debris from the surface before you glaze. [A]

STEP 2 Pick an interior glaze color. I’m using white on the inside of my
mugs, so I pour the glaze inside to approximately one-third of the way up,
do a quick rotation to fully coat the interior, and then I pour the glaze back
out. [B] I use a sponge to clean up any drips.

STEP 3 I’m using the same white glaze to coat the handle of my mugs, and to
save time, I’m dipping the handle in the bucket of glaze. [C] One dip should
suffice, then I’ll clean up the area around the handle. [D] For the rest of the
surface, I’ll be painting shapes and patterns with various colored glazes.

STEP 4 Starting with my planned pattern, [E] I pick my first color and start
painting my shapes. [F] I’m using either small-tipped detail brushes or
brushes with square heads, depending on the shapes I’m painting. I like to
embrace some drips and let my patterns blend in with one another, but I also
know to leave enough room at the bottom so that if my glazes drip, they
won’t drip all the way to the foot and run off the surface, sticking to the kiln
shelf. [G]

STEP 5 I repeat my patterns and switch colors when necessary until the
patterns are complete. [H] I clean up the base of each mug and any
unwanted glaze spots and prepare them for firing. [I]

STEP 6 Once fired, I gently hand-wash my cups before I use them and then
they’re ready. [J] A set of complimentary mugs or cups make a great set on
display in the kitchen, and your houseguests will love using your creations!

SET OF DINNER PLATES WITH INLAID CLAY DESIGNS

Inlaid clay designs are ideal for a finished surface that embraces patterns and natural
coloring and texture found within the clay. Using stoneware makes these a hearty option
for dinnerware, and a simple clear coat of glaze gives them a serviceable finish.
    I like to test my clear glaze on all of my clay bodies because sometimes the clear glaze
can take away some of the vivid colors of the clay. This helps me decide which clay will
look best when glazed clear and combined with other clay. For this project, I’m using
light, off-white, speckled stoneware clay with contrasting colors inlaid into the surface.
For these checkered patterns, I’m using black stoneware for the salad-sized plates and
white stoneware for the dinner-sized plates.
  Your patterns and shapes can change—they don’t have to be checkered. Play around
with dots and squares and have fun with organic shapes and blobs if you like as well!



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

At least 2 different clay bodies that shrink at the same rate and fire at the same
  temperature
Rolling pin or slab roller
Silicone rib tool
Needle tool for cutting
Plaster hump or slump molds or drape molds
Sponge
Bucket of water
Ware boards or pieces of canvas for your work surface
Lead-free, nontoxic, food-safe clear glaze
Large paintbrush for applying glaze

Instructions

STEP 1 I start by rolling a slab of my inlaid color clay (the slab that will be
cut and placed as the pattern) to a ⅛-inch (3 mm) thickness. [A] I compress
and smooth the surface with a silicone rib tool. Using my needle tool, I
handcut my shaped pieces, embracing the subtle differences and
imperfections in my cuts. [B] These shapes are cut small, and as they’re
pressed and rolled into the clay surface in the next steps, they’ll stretch out
and enlarge organically. I rarely aim for perfection with my cut shapes, but
you can if you like tight and clean designs. Set these cut-out shapes aside
with a sheet of plastic over the top so they don’t dry out too quickly.

STEP 2 Next, I use the other clay body to create the plate or the base color
that the shapes will be pressed into. I cut off a thick slab of this clay and roll
it out until it’s about 1-inch (2.5 cm) thick. [C]

STEP 3 Using the shapes I handcut from step 1, I lay out my pattern on the
top surface of the 1-inch (2.5 cm) thick base clay. I gently set these shapes
on top in the desired pattern, knowing that they’ll enlarge and stretch. [D] I
rotate the slab so that the clay is being stretched to fit my plate molds and
not stretching the clay too much in one direction; this would create thin
spots and irregular stretching of the shapes. [E] I’m aiming for a finished
thickness of ¼ inch (6 mm) for my plates, so I’m careful not to roll them
out too thin.

STEP 4 Once I’ve inlaid the shapes into the surface and I’ve reached my
desired thickness, I take my silicone rib tool and smooth any canvas texture
out, while also compressing my shapes and the inlaid clay. [F] Compression
is key to getting your inlaid clay to adhere. My smoothed slabs with the
inlaid patterns set up on ware boards for at least twenty-four hours, tightly
covered with plastic, before I cut the plates and press them onto their molds.
This allows the inlaid clay a chance to set up and be stronger when it comes
time to shape the plates.

STEP 5 After my slabs have set up, I cut my plates out for draping over the
molds. Using a salad-sized plate mold, I trace it over the slab and cut it out
with my needle tool. I lightly smooth the cut edge with a damp sponge and
drape the plate over the mold, compressing down until the surface is
completely and evenly set over the mold. [G] I set the molds aside for the
clay to set and firm up a bit—usually an hour or two. I repeat this until I
have enough plates, alternating between larger dinner plates and smaller,
salad-sized plates.





STEP 6 Once the plates have set up, I can flip them off the mold and onto a
ware board. I cover them with plastic so they can dry very slowly, for about
a week in my studio.

STEP 7 When the plates are in their greenware state, I use a damp sponge to
refine the edges and smooth out any fingerprints. [H] I bisque fire the plates
to their desired temperature.

STEP 8 After the plates are cooled and cleaned after bisque, I apply three
coats of clear glaze and prepare the plates for their glaze firing. [I]

STEP 9 Once they’re fired, I hand-wash the plates, and then it’s time to fix
my favorite meal and put them to use! [J]

HANDBUILT VASES WITH HEAVILY LAYERED GLAZES

We’ve covered the importance of testing glazes already, and once you feel you have a good
idea of how your glazes behave, then it’s time to start testing what happens when you
layer multiple glazes on the same piece.
   Layering too much glaze on a single piece can sometimes be problematic, and we don’t
want our glazes running onto the kiln shelves. But having a chance to discover what
happens when glazes are overlapped and layered on thick can be an exciting experience
and can open the doors to new surface design ideas. If you’re concerned about the final
results, you should create a test tile and plan out which glazes you want to try layering
there first before you commit to your vase’s entire surface.
  The surface of this vase began with a layer of peach-colored underglaze ovals, painted
on by hand, and then a layer of clear glaze over the peach ovals. After that, I started
adding layers and heavy drips of a matte speckled brown glaze as well as a drippy light
green glaze and a textured white crawl glaze—all layered in the same direction so that
drips were encouraged, to an extent. I finished this vase with a few dramatic drips of gold
luster too, embracing a heavy luster application to encourage the gold to move down the
surface of the vase as well. It suddenly became a statement vase, layer by layer by layer,
and I love the way it came out! I’ll be demonstrating on a smaller vase that I’ve finished in
the same style as this larger vase.



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

Bisque-fired vases, any form will do (handbuilt, wheel-thrown, or slip cast)
Sponge
Bucket of water
Various underglazes for layering (be sure to pick glazes you have some experience
  working with)
Assorted paintbrushes for applying glazes
Optional: underglaze pencil or pottery stamp
Optional: gold luster or other overglaze

Instructions

STEP 1 Start by lightly sponging any dust off the surface of your bisque-fired
vase. Choose the interior glaze color and pour the inside, rotating the vase
so that the walls are fully coated, [A] and then pour the glaze out. [B] One
poured interior coat of glaze will suffice.

STEP 2 Starting with underglaze, lay your first layer of color and pattern
with one or multiple colors of underglaze. After the two to three coats of
underglaze have dried, you can start with your first glaze color. [C] Start
layering in a concentric pattern with controlled shapes or have fun with
organic drips and splatters if you’re going for a less arranged look.

STEP 3 Keep layering your various colored glazes while also thinking about
varied textured glazes. Will layering a matte glaze change or affect the final
surface? Will adding four or more coats of glaze change the results you’re
used to achieving? Keep these design options in mind as you continue
layering your surface glazes. [D]

STEP 4 Once you feel you’ve layered as much glaze as you’re willing to
carefully wipe the foot clean and add your signature or stamp to the bottom.
Prepare your vase for firing in the kiln. [E]

STEP 5 You can opt for an additional layer of gold luster or other overglaze
[F], or you can call it good on its own.

DRIP AND SPLATTER PLATTER

A serving platter is one of my favorite things to make. I imagine a table filled with people
who love one another sharing a meal and passing the platter around so that everyone
gets a bite. Serving platters feel significant because they’re often the pieces that get
pulled out for special occasions, and I’m a big fan of celebrating special occasions. A
handmade ceramic platter with unique and stylized splatters of glaze can make a
statement at the table and is sure to impress your guests.
  My platter is oval, but I also love a large circular platter or even a long rectangular
platter. Don’t forget to keep the size of your kiln in mind when you’re first building your
platter. You’ll want to be sure it fits soundly in the kiln on a single shelf without bumping
the kiln walls.
   I’m using chunks of dried clay that I’ve picked off the rim of my glaze pints. I first tried
this technique when I was irritated by the amount of dried-up glazes I had accumulated
in my studio. Multiple pints and jars of clay had dried-up bits stuck around the rim, and it
took a lot of work to remix them back into a workable glaze. Using my needle tool, I
scrape off some of those dried chunks of glaze and sprinkle them onto the surface of my
platter so that they’ll fire into these bright drips and dots on the finished surface.



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

Bisque-fired ceramic platter
Sponge
Bucket of water
Various lead-free, nontoxic, food-safe glazes (I used a white base glaze with drips of
  navy blue)
Assorted paintbrushes for applying glazes
Needle tool for scraping dried glaze and applying glazes
Optional: underglaze pencil or pottery stamp

Instructions

STEP 1 Starting with a damp sponge, gently wipe off the surface of your
bisque-fired platter to remove any dust.

STEP 2 Using a large paintbrush, lay down your base coat. [A] White is
usually a safe bet as it generally accepts drips of other colors on top without
changing too drastically. (If you want to get adventurous, test out a few tiles
with different base layers and other colors of glaze dripped on top—you just
might find your next favorite glaze combination!) I apply three coats of my
white base glaze. I also sponge off the edges to clean up any glaze drips
from the bottom at this time.

STEP 3 Since we’re adding a more intricate glaze finish on the surface of the
platter, now is also a good time to go ahead and stamp or sign the bottom of
your platter (if you haven’t already). That way, you can ensure the surface
design won’t get messed up by flipping the platter over to sign it later. If
your platter was already stamped or signed when the clay was still wet, you
can skip this part.

STEP 4 I chose a deep navy blue glaze for my splatter drips, so using my
needle tool, I started by scraping off any dried pieces of glaze off the rim of
the pint and sprinkling those dried bits of glaze onto the platter’s surface.
[B] [C] Once you’re finished scattering the flecks of glaze, use a small brush
or your needle tool to dip into the wet glaze at the bottom of the pint jar.
Hold it over the platter and let the glaze fall in heavy drops onto the surface.
If you want more of a streaky splatter pattern (think Jackson Pollock), wave
your arm and brush or needle tool. A splatter design pattern looks very
different depending on your movements and the tool you use to apply the
glaze, so play around to uncover whatever splatter configurations are
calling your name on this project.

STEP 5 Once you’ve finalized the splatter look you’re going for and you’re
done treating the surface, you can set your piece aside for its kiln firing. [D]
As you move your platter or load it into the kiln, be careful to keep it flat
and not to tip the platter. Your loose glaze chunks might fall off, and you
don’t want those falling into the kiln or onto the kiln shelves.

STEP 6 Once your platter is cooled and out of the kiln, clean up any kiln
shelf debris from the bottom. Hand-wash your new serving tray and find an
occasion that calls for plentiful platters and people you love gathered
together! [E]

PLANTERS WITH ADDITIVE DESIGNS

A planter is one of the best functional pieces that allow you to get wild with shaped
attachments and additive designs on the outer surface. You won’t be using this piece in
the same way you would use a plate or a cup, so an intricate design attached to the outer
surface is suitable for things like planters that sit on a shelf or a plant stand. Not to
mention, it’s a beautiful way to embellish your ceramic pieces.
  One of the more important things to keep in mind when you’re attaching two pieces of
clay together is making sure both pieces are at the same stage of drying or have the same
level of moisture. If the attachment pieces are drier than the clay they’re being attached
to, they’ll shrink at a faster rate than the other piece, causing the attachment to crack at
the point of contact. You want the attached pieces to dry at the same rate as the pot
they’re attached to.
  For my planters, I’ve used a simple rectangular shape that I’ve cut and repeatedly
attached all around the exterior wall. I call them tabs. I use a different-colored glaze for
each tab and embrace the raw red texture of the rest of the clay. The finished result is a
colorful rainbow planter that becomes a statement piece no matter what plant lives in
there!



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

Clay for handbuilding your planter
Rolling pin
Needle tool for scoring and making attachments
Slip brush
Various glazes
Assorted paintbrushes for applying glazes
Sponge
Bucket of water
Optional: pencil, ruler, and stencils or paper templates for tracing your designs

Instructions

STEP 1 I’m a handbuilder at heart, so I’m starting by coil building a large-
sized planter. [A] [B] [C] Once I’ve built the planter to my desired size, I can
cut my shaped attachment pieces.

STEP 2 Next, I roll a small slab to cut my shaped attachment pieces out of. I
roll my slab to about ⅛ inch (3 mm) thick and start cutting out rectangular
tabs that I’ll attach in a line all the way around the planter. I want my rolled
slab to be the same consistency as the planter, so make sure the attached
pieces aren’t too dry or too wet in comparison to the piece they’ll be
attached to. To make things easier, I score an entire side of the slab, and
then I use templates to trace designs or cut shapes freehand out of the slab.
[D] [E] Pull up your shapes and cover them in plastic so they don’t dry out
too quickly while you’re working.

STEP 3 I’m attaching the rectangular tabs all around the center portion of the
planter, so I size up my first tab and score the planter where the tab will
attach. With a small amount of slip, I adhere the shaped piece to the planter
with careful compressions, and I use my slip brush to clean up my
attachment. [F] [G] Repeat until all of your shapes are attached in the
desired pattern and cover your planter with plastic to slowly dry over the
next several days. Slow drying is key.

STEP 4 Once your planter has been carefully dried and refined, you can
prepare it for bisque firing. [H]

STEP 5 Now, it’s time to glaze. Your attachment pieces can be finished in
whatever color palette and combinations you dream of. I went for a rainbow
effect, painting each rectangular tab in a different color. You could pick a
single color glaze or alternate colors on each tab like I have. Pick your own
designs and colors. I’m brushing the glazes on with a paintbrush that is
about the same width as my attachment shapes. [I] Most of my glazes need
three coats of application.





STEP 6 Clean up any drips or glaze from around the edges of your glazed
attachment shapes with a small sponge and prepare your piece for the kiln.

STEP 7 Once your planter is fired, find the right plant that needs a new home
and admire your handiwork! [J] [K]
